title: Statue of John Hope, 4th Earl of Hopetoun
address: Forecourt of Dundas House, 36 St Andrew Square, Edinburgh EH2 2YB
about_site_text: A life-size bronze of John Hope, 4th Earl of Hopetoun (1765-1823), the general who took command of the British army at Corunna after Sir John Moore was killed. Sculpted by Thomas Campbell, it stands in the railed forecourt of Dundas House, long the head office of the Royal Bank of Scotland. Hope wears a Roman toga rather than uniform and stands beside a horse with its head bowed - a pedestrian figure, not a mounted one. A stepped granite plinth carries a drum-ended bronze pedestal, its inscription written by Sir Walter Scott.
interesting_fact: It was never meant to be here. Edinburgh commissioned the statue in 1824 for Charlotte Square, then judged it unsuitable; it went unplaced for years until the bank accepted it in 1834 and set it in its own forecourt. The accidental siting produced the square's best in-joke: the Earl stands looking west across the gardens directly at the Melville Monument and Henry Dundas - who was his brother-in-law, having married the Earl's sister Lady Jane Hope in 1793. In 2020 the statue was drawn into Edinburgh's review of monuments with slavery links, over Hope's part in crushing Fedon's rebellion in Grenada in 1795-96.

title: Lion of Scotland
about_site_text: A 20-tonne recumbent lion hand-carved from a single boulder of pink granite by sculptor Ronald Rae, moved here in 2010. The stone is Corrennie granite from Aberdeenshire and the finished animal runs to roughly 17 feet long and 8 feet high. It was first sited in Holyrood Park, on the ground between the Palace of Holyroodhouse and the new Scottish Parliament, placed there deliberately beneath Arthur's Seat - a hill long read as a lion in its own right.
interesting_fact: It's been voted Edinburgh's best-loved sculpture - and took over a year to carve using hand tools only, with no power tools at any stage. When the Holyrood loan was due to expire in 2008, Scottish Blue Badge guides raised a petition and thousands of residents and visitors signed it; that won a two-year reprieve, and on 25 April 2010 the lion made the mile-long journey across town to St Andrew Square Garden. It came on loan rather than by purchase, financed by Essential Edinburgh and private sponsors, and Rae has said he hopes the city will one day buy it outright. Technically, it is still a visitor.

title: Melville Monument
about_site_text: A fluted Doric column over 45 metres tall, inspired by Trajan's Column in Rome and topped with a statue of Henry Dundas, 1st Viscount Melville. Built 1821-27 and weighing around 1,500 tons, the monument was engineered with help from Robert Stevenson - the lighthouse-building grandfather of novelist Robert Louis Stevenson, brought in because nothing this large had been attempted in Scotland before. The design was William Burn's, and the roughly 15-foot figure on top was carved by Robert Forrest to a model by Sir Francis Chantrey.
interesting_fact: Dundas was so politically powerful in late-18th-century Scotland he was nicknamed 'The Uncrowned King of Scotland' - and this monument is literally the 'big man in the sky' the game's own clue points players toward. In 1806 he became the last person ever impeached in the UK, for misappropriating public funds; a plaque added to the monument in 2021 also addresses his role in delaying the abolition of the slave trade. The £8,000 bill was met by subscription from the officers and men of the Royal Navy, which Dundas had run as First Lord of the Admiralty from 1804.

title: Paddington Bear Statue
address: St Andrew Square Gardens (near 42 St Andrew Sq), Edinburgh
about_site_text: A bronze Paddington Bear, marmalade sandwich in hand, sitting on a bench in the garden. He is deliberately sized to leave one clear gap beside him, which is the whole point of him: the trail was built around the photograph you are about to take. Worth noting where he is sitting - St Andrew Square Garden was private railed ground, reserved for the householders around it, for well over two centuries, and only opened to the general public in 2008.
interesting_fact: Unveiled 9 Oct 2024 as part of the national 'Paddington Visits' trail (tied to the Paddington in Peru film) - one of 23 across the UK and Ireland, strung out between John O'Groats and Land's End and each hand-painted in the red hat and blue duffle coat. Michael Bond bought the lone unsold teddy that started it all on Christmas Eve 1956, as a present for his wife; 'A Bear Called Paddington' followed on 13 October 1958. The luggage label round the bear's neck - 'Please look after this bear' - came straight from Bond's memory of wartime evacuee children arriving at London stations with tags tied to their coats.

title: National Portrait Gallery
about_site_text: Scotland's national portrait collection, housed in a red sandstone Gothic Revival pile on the north side of Queen Street. Robert Rowand Anderson designed it; it was built 1885-90 and opened in 1889, the stone quarried at Corsehill near Annan in Dumfriesshire. Four octagonal corner turrets with crocketed pinnacles frame a facade studded with niche statues of famous Scots. It was built as a double building - the portrait gallery in the east wing, the National Museum of Antiquities in the west - sharing one Great Hall as a common entrance.
interesting_fact: Nobody was supposed to know who paid for it. In 1882 an anonymous 10,000 pound gift arrived to "set on foot" a national portrait gallery; the donor quietly kept paying until the bill reached roughly 70,000 pounds, and his identity was revealed only on opening day in 1889 - John Ritchie Findlay, proprietor of The Scotsman. It was the first building in the world purpose-built as a portrait gallery. Inside, the Great Hall's arcaded balcony carries William Hole's processional frieze of 155 Scots running backwards in time from Thomas Carlyle to the Stone Age, beneath a ceiling of over 2,000 gold stars.

title: The Capital Building
address: The Capital Building, 12-13 St Andrew Square, Edinburgh EH2 2AF
about_site_text: An Art Deco outlier on the corner of St Andrew Square and George Street, built 1938-40 as the head office of the Caledonian Insurance Company to designs by Leslie Grahame Thomson with Frank J Connell. Polished black granite at street level gives way to warm sandstone above, cut with strong vertical lines and geometric detail. The splayed corner entrance is flanked by two outsized bronzes by Alexander Carrick. Inside are a marble-lined hall, an imperial staircase and a roof-lit rotunda. Reportedly Category A listed, now multi-tenant offices over a restaurant.
interesting_fact: The two bronzes over the door are an insurance advert in metal. Carrick's figures are "Safety" - a man shielding a young girl - and "Security" - a woman with a baby and a boy: not civic virtues, but precisely the two things a Caledonian Insurance policy claimed to sell, cast at twice life size above the counter where you bought one. The theme carries indoors, where William Wilson's stained glass in the stairwell depicts commercial trades rather than scripture. The building was finished just as war halted Edinburgh construction, making it one of the New Town's very few full-blooded Art Deco set pieces.

title: James Clerk Maxwell statue
address: Central reservation, east end of George Street at St Andrew Square, Edinburgh EH2 2LL
about_site_text: A seated bronze of the physicist James Clerk Maxwell (1831-1879) by Alexander Stoddart, unveiled 25 November 2008 on the central reservation at the east end of George Street, facing west. Maxwell is shown in Victorian dress at roughly the age he died, holding the spinning colour top he used to investigate colour vision, with his terrier Toby at his feet. Bronze reliefs on the granite plinth show Newton with his prism and Einstein with a warped-spacetime sheet, and a plaque carries Maxwell's equations.
interesting_fact: The four equations on the plinth are not the ones Maxwell wrote. His 1865 formulation ran to twenty equations in twenty variables; the compact vector form the world now calls "Maxwell's equations" was boiled down by Oliver Heaviside two decades later, after Maxwell was dead. The site is apt for a second reason: the Royal Society of Edinburgh, which commissioned the statue and sits a block west, first published Maxwell at fourteen - his 1846 paper on oval curves had to be read aloud to the Society by Professor James Forbes, because a boy that age could not present it himself.

title: Thistle Court
about_site_text: Two pairs of modest semi-detached houses facing each other across a small grass court, built in 1767 - the oldest surviving buildings in the whole New Town. They are plain two-storey-and-attic classical houses of sandstone rubble, some of it red, with ashlar dressings: no columns, no pediment, nothing whatsoever to announce that Edinburgh's grandest building project started here. All four are now Category A listed, and the court is thought to have been called Rose Court originally.
interesting_fact: They exist because developer John Young simply ignored James Craig's rigid grid plan and built houses facing each other instead of a terraced row - possibly the oldest semi-detached houses in Scotland. The town council had dangled a £20 premium for the first builder to break ground in the New Town, and Young collected it. The rest of Thistle Street took another twenty-odd years to fill up, put up as plain craft workers' dwellings and workshops - the cheap seats directly behind George Street's mansions - and Craig named it for Scotland's emblem to pair with Rose Street, named for England's.

title: The Dome
about_site_text: Built around 1847 to a design by architect David Rhind in the Graeco-Roman style, on the site of the former Physicians' Hall. Its hexastyle Corinthian portico is 95 feet wide with six 35-foot columns, topped by a sculpted pediment by Alexander Handyside Ritchie. Now a Category A listed building, it takes its name from the large glass dome lighting the banking hall inside. Ritchie's pediment group is Fruitfulness attended by Trade and Navigation - the same group the Commercial Bank engraved on its own banknotes, so Scots carried this building around in their pockets.
interesting_fact: The bank that built this grand headquarters eventually merged into the very same Royal Bank of Scotland whose own head office - Dundas House - is the first stop on this walk: once a rival across town, now part of the same institution. The Commercial Bank became the National Commercial Bank in 1959 and was absorbed by RBS ten years later. The Physicians' Hall it replaced was designed by James Craig, who planned the New Town; its foundation stone was laid in 1776, and when it came down in January 1844 the workmen opened that stone and found silver medals sealed inside.

title: St Andrew's and St George's West Church
about_site_text: Built in 1784 as St Andrew's Church - the first church built in the New Town. The design was won in competition by Captain Andrew Frazer of the Royal Engineers, then chief army engineer for Scotland, working with Robert Kay, and its oval interior was the first elliptical church plan in Britain - partly a virtue made of necessity, since the leftover plot was too shallow for a conventional nave. The ceiling was lifted from Robert Wood's 'Ruins of Palmyra' of 1753, with Scottish thistles worked in. The 51-metre steeple was an afterthought, added in 1787.
interesting_fact: The site was originally earmarked for Dundas House (now the RBS HQ landmark) before it was swapped for the church - Sir Lawrence Dundas quietly bought up the square's east side before Craig's plan could be enforced, and the church was bumped along George Street instead. The steeple holds eight bells cast in 1788 at London's Whitechapel foundry, the oldest complete ring in Scotland. And on 18 May 1843 this was the room where the Disruption happened: around a third of the ministers at the General Assembly walked out and founded the Free Church of Scotland.

title: Caledonian Insurance Building
about_site_text: A grand former insurance office designed by David Bryce, 1839-40, remodelling one of the plain 1780s townhouses that originally filled this side of George Street. It was worked over again in 1879-80, and the Caledonian finally moved out in 1939, selling the premises to the George Hotel next door; the military promptly requisitioned them for the rest of the war. Bryce's doorway is now the hotel's main entrance, and the old insurance hall survives inside as the King's Hall.
interesting_fact: One of several bank and insurance buildings that made St Andrew Square and George Street 'possibly the richest area of its size in Scotland' in the 19th century. The Caledonian, founded in Edinburgh in June 1805, is usually called the oldest Scottish insurance company - and it was born out of pure spite. A man named Forrest Alexander had a £600 fire claim thrown out by his English insurers because his renewal ran one day late, so he set about starting a Scottish one instead. The painter Sir Henry Raeburn sat on the board and designed the company's policy heading, which stayed in use until 1838.

title: Royal Society of Edinburgh
about_site_text: Home of Scotland's National Academy of Science and Letters since 1908/09 - a Category A building with a distinctive green cupola. The present block went up in 1908-09 to a design by J M Dick Peddie, faced in fossil-bearing Portland stone from Dorset over a base course of Creetown granite: paler, harder and glossier than the local sandstone on either side of it, which is why the frontage reads slightly cold next to its neighbours. The Society bought the site from the Edinburgh Life Assurance Company with the help of a £25,000 government grant.
interesting_fact: Founded 1783 in imitation of London's Royal Society; before settling here it moved through several homes across the city, including a spell at 40-42 George Street just down the road. Its earliest lodgings, from 1807, were in the Physicians' Hall - which stood on the site of The Dome, a few doors east on this same walk. Adam Smith, Joseph Black and James Hutton all sat on the first Council, and it was to this Society that Hutton read his 'Theory of the Earth', the paper that effectively invented deep geological time. The first women Fellows were not elected until 1949.

title: Susan Ferrier's Home
about_site_text: Home of novelist Susan Ferrier from 1784 to around 1830. She was two years old when the family moved in - the house was numbered 11 at the time - and she stayed for most of her adult life, writing all three of her novels under this roof. Her father James Ferrier was a Writer to the Signet and a Principal Clerk of the Court of Session, which put him at the next desk to Walter Scott and gave his daughter a standing invitation into Edinburgh's literary establishment. Today, this specific townhouse has been absorbed into the historic, luxury hotel InterContinental Edinburgh The George.
interesting_fact: Sometimes called 'the Scottish Jane Austen', Ferrier was a contemporary and friend of Sir Walter Scott. All three of her novels appeared anonymously and she was not publicly named as their author until 1851, three years before her death. The fees tell you how well they sold: Blackwood paid £150 for 'Marriage' in 1818, and by 'Destiny' in 1831 Robert Cadell was handing over £1,700, a small fortune for a novel then. Scott rated her company as much as her books, calling her conversation 'the least exigeant of any author, female at least'. Failing eyesight made her a recluse; she is buried at St Cuthbert's.

title: King George IV Statue
address: Junction of George St and Hanover St, Edinburgh
about_site_text: Commemorates George IV's visit to Edinburgh in August 1822 - the first visit by a reigning monarch in around 170 years. Sculpted by Sir Francis Chantrey. The king is shown in full Highland dress, part of the tartan pageantry Walter Scott stage-managed around the whole visit, and he stands on a massive stepped ashlar plinth carrying just five words: GEORGE IV VISITED SCOTLAND MDCCCXXII. Chantrey picked this crossing for it himself. Category A listed.
interesting_fact: Chantrey also sculpted the William Pitt statue at the far end of this leg - same sculptor, two statues, one walk. Make that three: the figure of Henry Dundas on top of the Melville Monument back in St Andrew Square was carved by Robert Forrest from a Chantrey model, so Chantrey effectively bookends and centres this entire route. The statue was unveiled on 26 November 1831, by which point George IV had been dead for well over a year - he died in June 1830 - so the king being congratulated here never saw the thing. Chantrey left his fortune to found the Chantrey Bequest, which still buys art for the nation.

title: The Assembly Rooms
about_site_text: Opened 1787, the most important surviving building of its type in the UK - Category A listed, still an events venue today. It was designed by John Henderson, who won the competition for it in 1781 and then died in February 1786 before it was finished, and paid for by public subscription at a cost of over £6,000 on a site the town council handed over for nothing. The opening event, on 11 January 1787, was the Caledonian Hunt Ball. The great portico came later, in 1818, and the Music Hall behind it in 1843.
interesting_fact: In August 1822 it hosted the Peers Ball for King George IV's visit to Edinburgh - the same visit commemorated by the George IV statue a few doors down this same leg. Five years later, at a Theatrical Fund dinner here in February 1827, Walter Scott finally admitted in public that he was the author of the Waverley novels, a secret he had kept for thirteen years - a toast to 'the Author of Waverley' left him no way out and he stood up and owned it. Dickens and Thackeray both read here afterwards, and since 1981 it has been one of the big Fringe venues.

title: Pink Sandstone Among Yellow Free-Stone
about_site_text: Former Dowells Auctioneers, built 1907-08 - the one building on this stretch built in pale pink sandstone rather than the local yellow/cream sandstone everyone else used. The architects were John Nichol Scott and Alexander Lorne Campbell, and behind the front block sit two plain top-lit auction rooms, the eastern one of real historic interest. Dowell's ran sales here for generations; its catalogues and roup rolls, from 1879 onwards, are now held by the National Library of Scotland.
interesting_fact: The pink is New Red Sandstone from Locharbriggs near Dumfries, and it is here for a reason. Most of the New Town was built from Craigleith quarry on the city's own north-western edge, but by the Edwardian period the railways had made Dumfriesshire stone cheap to haul seventy miles north, and red stone was fashionable besides. So the odd one out is not just a different colour - it is a different rock entirely, laid down in a Permian desert something like eighty million years after the swampy Carboniferous sands that make up its neighbours. Craigleith worked from 1615 and did not close until 1942.

title: Hidden Back-Lane White Tiles
about_site_text: White glazed brick tiling lining a New Town back lane - a common Georgian/Victorian trick to bounce light down narrow service lanes with no direct sun. The lanes themselves are pure Craig: every one of his blocks is cut through by a mews lane, lined with stables and coach houses so carriages never appeared at the front door. Rose Street North Lane served the discreet back entrances of the Princes Street houses. Well into the 19th century some also held byres for the cows that supplied the surrounding households with milk.
interesting_fact: Confirmed on-site with a real photo - white glazed brick pillars between the windows, plus a decorative black-and-white diamond-pattern tile band lower down. Glazed brick like this was mass-produced from the 1860s onwards by fireclay firms like Burmantofts of Leeds, and sunless spaces such as lightwells were routinely lined with it to reflect daylight deeper in. It had a second use in a coal-smoke city that called itself Auld Reekie - a glazed face sheds soot and can be sluiced clean with a bucket, which is also why it lined the stables and dairies these lanes held.

title: The Giant Caryatids
about_site_text: Built 1903-07 as the flagship headquarters of the Professional and Civil Service Supply Association - a Victorian trading cooperative where civil servants, teachers and clerks paid a small membership fee for discounted wholesale goods, until they outgrew their original Frederick Street shop and commissioned this statement building instead. Architect Sir John James Burnet, a leading figure of Edwardian Baroque in Scotland, faced it in polished cream sandstone banded with dark granite, pushing the top floor back into a dramatic recessed gallery.
interesting_fact: Rather than plain stone pillars, Burnet held up that 5th-floor gallery with a row of giant carved caryatids - draped female figures known as the 'Four Seasons Facade', each one carved with details representing Spring, Summer, Autumn or Winter. Classical caryatids are meant to look as if they're effortlessly carrying the building's weight, and Burnet used the trick to make a six-storey stone block feel light at its highest point. The cooperative era gave way to a long spell as a National Westminster Bank branch; the interior is now WeWork offices, but the four seasons still watch over George Street exactly as Burnet intended.

title: Micro-Lighthouse Above the Doorway
about_site_text: Headquarters of the Northern Lighthouse Board since 1832. Look up at the first-floor window directly above the door: a detailed, working miniature lighthouse model (a replica of Bell Rock Lighthouse) juts from the facade, lamp still revolving. It was built on the premises and has been running since 1950. The house itself dates from 1786 and is Category A listed, and the body inside is still the lighthouse authority for the whole of Scotland and the Isle of Man.
interesting_fact: Robert Louis Stevenson's own family were the famous lighthouse engineers who worked for this very body - a second RLS thread on this route, alongside the Chantrelle case above which is said to have inspired Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde. Eight Stevensons across four generations designed close to a hundred Scottish lighthouses between 1790 and 1940. The original of the model above your head is the one that made the family name: Bell Rock, built 1807-10 by RLS's grandfather Robert on a reef eleven miles out in the North Sea that vanishes under water at every high tide. Its lamp was first lit on 1 February 1811 and the masonry has never needed replacing.

title: Freemasons' Hall
about_site_text: Headquarters of the Grand Lodge of Scotland since the mid-19th century. Current building 1911-12 by Alexander Hunter Crawford, a prominent freemason himself - it is reckoned his most important work and is Category A listed. It replaced an earlier hall of 1858 on the same site by David Bryce, the architect of the Caledonian Insurance building back at the St Andrew Square end of this walk, which means two generations of the same commission sit on one street.
interesting_fact: The facade carries a large statue of St Andrew, and the building holds a museum of Masonic treasures open to the public. The saint was carved by Henry Snell Gamley, whose King Edward VII stands in the forecourt of Holyrood Palace and whose figures decorate the Usher Hall. The Grand Lodge inside governs Scottish Freemasonry and dates its own founding to 1736; on its roll at No 1 is the Lodge of Edinburgh (Mary's Chapel), whose minute of 31 July 1599 is the oldest surviving record of any lodge still working anywhere in the world. From 1947 the hall doubled as a concert venue for the new Edinburgh International Festival.

title: Early Modernist Steel Anomaly
about_site_text: Built 1924-25 for Cleghorn's Department Store to a design by Alfred George Lochhead, this four-storey ashlar building broke every rule of James Craig's 1767 New Town plan, which demanded uniform classical stone facades and traditional load-bearing masonry. Lochhead hid a structural steel frame inside instead, letting the building open into wider window spans and larger open retail floors than anything else on the block - Early Modernism smuggled behind a polished cream sandstone front.
interesting_fact: The splayed corner entrance carries a striking Egyptian Revival doorcase in polished red and black granite - a style that swept the world after Tutankhamun's tomb was discovered in 1922, arriving here within two years. Higher up, a Lorimerian scrolled pediment nods back to the Georgian neighbours it otherwise defies. In a later rework, architects CDA added a glass-and-steel penthouse floor deliberately built in the spirit of the 1920s frame beneath it - approved by Historic Scotland - now home to the rooftop restaurant Oloroso, with panoramic views over the Castle and the Forth.

title: Thomas Chalmers Statue
address: George Street at Castle Street, Edinburgh
about_site_text: A standing bronze of Dr Thomas Chalmers (1780-1847), theologian and reformer who became the first Moderator of the Free Church of Scotland. Sculpted by Sir John Steell and unveiled in 1878, he stands robed as Moderator with a large open Bible on his left forearm, his right hand marking the page. The bronze rises from a stepped red granite plinth carrying a bare inscription: "THOMAS CHALMERS DD DCL BORN 1780 DIED 1847" - no list of achievements, just the facts of a life that reshaped the Church of Scotland.
interesting_fact: Retrace your steps and you've already passed the building where his story peaked. On 18 May 1843, at St Andrew's and St George's Church back along George Street, Chalmers led roughly a third of the ministers at the Church of Scotland's General Assembly out in protest at state interference in church appointments - the "Disruption." Outside, he was cheered through the streets to found the Free Church of Scotland as its first Moderator, a sustentation fund already drawn up to support the hundreds of ministers who had just given up manse and salary. This statue, raised three decades later, put him back on the street where it happened.

title: View Down Castle Street to the Castle
address: Castle Street at George Street, Edinburgh
about_site_text: Castle Street was one of three cross-streets in James Craig's New Town plan whose names weren't picked at random - alongside Frederick Street, after King George III's father Prince Frederick, and Hanover Street, after the royal house, Castle Street was aligned and named because Edinburgh Castle sits squarely at its far end. Standing at the George Street junction and looking south, the fortress rises above the street on its volcanic crag, framed by tenements on either side - a piece of 18th-century town planning still working exactly as intended over two centuries later.
interesting_fact: Craig's original 1766 prize-winning competition entry was far fussier than what actually got built: a diagonal layout of radiating streets around a central square, loosely inspired by the Union flag. The town council judged it impractical, and Craig reworked it into the plainer grid of parallel streets that exists today - the very plan whose cross-streets, including this one, were given these deliberate, view-aligned names.

title: Walter Scott's House
about_site_text: A plain, handsome three-storey Georgian townhouse just off George Street, built for Sir Walter Scott and his family's winter home from 1801 to 1826. It was here, at what he affectionately called "the cabin," that Scott wrote the bulk of the Waverley novels that made him the best-selling author in Europe, working before his day job at the Court of Session even began. Category A listed, the house remains a private residence today, its exterior essentially unchanged since Scott's time.
interesting_fact: In January 1826 Scott's printing and publishing partnerships collapsed under debts of well over £100,000, and rather than declare bankruptcy he spent the rest of his life writing to pay it off - a decision that cost him his health. He recorded leaving Castle Street for the last time in his journal: "This morning I leave No. 39 Castle Street for the last time... So farewell, poor 39." J.M.W. Turner painted the house in 1834, two years after Scott's death, titling the work simply "Former Residence of Walter Scott."

title: The Oxford Bar
about_site_text: The Oxford Bar, tucked down Young Street just off Castle Street, is a small, unshowy New Town pub that apparently became a public house in 1811 - though records also show it trading as a confectioner's shop as late as 1843, and it was formally disponed to wine and spirits merchant Andrew Wilson in 1893, after which it stayed a bar for good. Category B listed since 1966, it keeps its original compartmentalised layout: a central corridor with small rooms either side, one now opened up through an archway. No music, no fruit machines, no television - just pies, rolls, and a well-kept range of beer and whisky.
interesting_fact: This unassuming bar is world-famous among crime fiction readers as the real-life local of Ian Rankin's Inspector Rebus, drinking here on the page since the character's 1987 debut. Rankin chose it partly because it was a genuine haunt of off-duty police officers, and the pub has stayed famously indifferent to its own fame - no Rebus merchandise, no themed decor. Past regulars have included poet Sydney Goodsir Smith; Monty Python's Michael Palin dropped in back in 1978, years before Rebus turned the place into a pilgrimage site for readers worldwide.

title: Church of Scotland Offices
about_site_text: A big, Scandinavian-flavoured office block built 1909-11 for the United Free Church of Scotland, designed by Edinburgh architect Sydney Mitchell. Its steep double-pitched mansard roof and heavy stonework read closer to Stockholm than to the Georgian street around it. A matching bookshop extension went up next door at 119 George Street in the 1930s, and the complex has held a chapel and staff canteen since it was built. Category A listed, it remains the administrative headquarters of the Church of Scotland.
interesting_fact: The building was finished eighteen years before its own name became accurate. It was built for the United Free Church of Scotland - descended from the Free Church that Thomas Chalmers founded after the 1843 Disruption, whose statue stands a short walk back along this street - and only became genuinely "Church of Scotland offices" when the two churches reunited in 1929, healing a rift that had run for generations. A planned matching extension on the west side was never built, though the church did buy the neighbouring building at 123 George Street.

title: Kimpton Charlotte Square Hotel
address: 38 Charlotte Square, Edinburgh (corner of George Street)
about_site_text: A row of grand Georgian townhouses at the corner where George Street opens into Charlotte Square, designed by Robert Adam in 1791 as part of his unified palace-front scheme for the square, and reworked in 1810 by his successor as the Crown's Scottish architect, Robert Reid. Two of the houses, Nos 38 and 39, were knocked together to form a hotel in the 1870s, with more of the terrace absorbed over later decades. Long known as the Roxburghe Hotel, it was rebranded in 2019 as the Kimpton Charlotte Square, though the Adam-Reid facade above street level is unchanged.
interesting_fact: The address hides one of the New Town's stranger continuities: architects kept adapting the shell of Adam's 1791 townhouses rather than replacing them, as the building passed from private residence to hotel through several names and refits, including a 1939 remodel that finally opened up the blind ground-floor windows facing the square. Guests today sleep behind the same pilastered facade Adam drew for householders who never imagined a hotel there - and it looks out across the gardens at the domed former church Robert Reid designed after inheriting Adam's unbuilt commission for the opposite side of the square.

title: Prince Albert Memorial
about_site_text: A 30-foot bronze equestrian statue of Prince Albert in Field Marshal's uniform, rearing on a granite pedestal at the centre of Charlotte Square Gardens. Sculpted by Sir John Steell, who won the commission after Albert's sudden death from typhoid in December 1861, it was unveiled by Queen Victoria in person on 17 August 1876 - Steell was knighted by the Queen on the spot. Four bronze figure groups ring the base, each by a different sculptor: William Brodie's Nobility, Clark Stanton's Army and Navy, and D.W. Stevenson's Labour and Science and Learning.
interesting_fact: It took Victoria fifteen years to unveil a monument to her own husband, by which point several other Albert memorials already stood elsewhere in Britain. The horse was cast from a single piece with no visible joins, reckoned a technical feat at the time. And the garden it stands in is still private: unlike St Andrew Square at the other end of this walk, opened to the public in 2008, Charlotte Square Gardens remain locked and keyholder-only, open to everyone only a handful of days a year - so the statue is usually viewed through railings, not up close.

title: West Register House
about_site_text: A great domed building closing the west side of Charlotte Square, built 1811-14 as St George's Church to a design by Robert Reid, reworking an earlier scheme for the same site that Robert Adam had drawn up before his death in 1792. The foundation stone was laid on 14 May 1811, and the church opened on 5 June 1814 with seating for around 1,600 worshippers beneath a green copper dome and gilt cupola rising some 160 feet, deliberately styled to echo St Paul's Cathedral in London. Its pulpit, carved in Spanish mahogany, stood a full 20 feet high.
interesting_fact: The £18,000 budget nearly doubled to £33,000 by completion - not the last time this building would be rebuilt from within. St George's closed as a congregation in 1964, merging with St Andrew's Church further along George Street (where Chalmers led the 1843 Disruption), and by 1970 the sacred interior had been gutted and replaced with five storeys of fireproof archive stacks. It reopened as West Register House, one of the two homes of the National Records of Scotland, still holding some of the nation's oldest legal documents under the dome once built for hymn-singing.

title: The Georgian House
about_site_text: A National Trust for Scotland museum recreating a New Town townhouse at the height of Georgian fashion, in a house built in 1796 for John Lamont, 18th Chief of Clan Lamont, who lived here until 1815. From 1889 it was home to theologian Rev Alexander Whyte, minister of nearby Free St George's, and his wife Jane, who raised eight children within it. The Marquess of Bute acquired the house in 1927; on the 5th Marquess's death in 1956, Nos 5, 6 and 7 passed to the National Trust in part settlement of death duties, restored and opened to the public in 1975.
interesting_fact: For decades before it became a museum, No.7 served as an antique dealer's showroom - the very trade the house now exists to interpret, minus the historical accuracy. Lamont bought the newly built house for a little over £1,800 and sold it twenty years later for £3,000, trying and failing to offset debts that helped push his clan's finances into decline. The house stands directly next to No.6, Bute House, official residence of Scotland's First Minister since 1999 - a debt-ridden chief's townhouse sharing a garden wall with the seat of the devolved Scottish government.

title: Bute House
about_site_text: Designed by Robert Adam as part of his grand vision for Charlotte Square in 1791 - though Adam died the following year, before it was finished. Number 6 has been the official residence of Scotland's First Minister since 1999. The plot was first sold in 1792 to Orlando Hart, a shoemaker and prominent Edinburgh town councillor. The building later spent nearly 20 years as a hotel, and the Marquesses of Bute owned it for over 60 years before it was preserved for the nation in 1966.
interesting_fact: In 1832, the exiled King Charles X of France stayed here briefly while it was operating as a hotel - some of the hotel's original brass lettering is still visible on the building today.

title: Rose Street (West End)
address: Rose Street at South Charlotte Street, Edinburgh
about_site_text: Rose Street begins here, at its western end, meeting South Charlotte Street just around the corner from Charlotte Square. Laid out by James Craig in 1767 as a modest service lane behind George Street's grand townhouses, it's this trade character - not the architecture above - that gives Rose Street its real fame today: a thousand-metre run stacked with pubs, bars and restaurants, said to hold twelve traditional pubs on the well-known 'Rose Street Challenge' crawl route alone, plus just as many other bars besides. The crawl traditionally starts right here on the left-hand side at Scott's, 202 Rose Street - said to date back to 1790 and named for a formidable 19th-century landlady, 'Ma Scott', whose reputation is still advertised on the pub's own sign today.
interesting_fact: Victorian Edinburgh regarded the whole street as faintly disreputable after dark, and the pub scene that grew up along it eventually gave Rose Street its modern nickname, the 'Amber Mile.' The full crawl runs from Scott's here all the way to the Abbotsford at the street's far end - roughly one drinking establishment every 80 metres along the route. Pedestrianised by the 1970s, Rose Street runs some 1,000 metres in total to St Andrew Square; this walk follows only its westernmost stretch.

title: Charlotte Chapel / Rose Theatre
about_site_text: A plain, dignified stone hall near the western end of Rose Street, built in 1912 as Charlotte Chapel to a design by J A Arnott and J Inch Morrison, seating 1,000 worshippers on the site of an earlier 18th-century chapel. The congregation was founded in January 1808 by evangelist Christopher Anderson, who began preaching in the Pleasance before outgrowing that hall and relocating his church here. Category B listed, the building served as a working Baptist chapel for over a century, its restrained exterior giving little away about the busy congregational life that filled it inside.
interesting_fact: In 2016 the congregation, grown too large again, moved out to a former Church of Scotland building on Shandwick Place, leaving this hall empty for the first time in two centuries. Danish choreographer Peter Schaufuss bought the deconsecrated chapel that year for 1.8 million pounds and reopened it in 2017 as the Rose Theatre, now a year-round performing arts venue and Fringe hub built across four stages inside the old chapel's shell. As of 2026, a hotel conversion with a rooftop bar has already been approved for the building - so the theatre inside today may prove just one more phase in a longer story.

title: Beachcomber by George Mackay Brown
about_site_text: Set into the arched windows of a former telephone exchange near the western end of Rose Street, seven laser-cut steel panels illustrate all seven verses of Orcadian poet George Mackay Brown's 1971 poem 'Beachcomber,' one verse per window. Artist Astrid Jaekel designed the piece first as intricate hand-cut paper before Pentland Precision Engineering translated it into weatherproof steel, commissioned around 2012-13 by Essential Edinburgh as part of a project to regenerate and celebrate the street's cultural heritage - a nod to the 'Rose Street Poets' who once drank in its pubs.
interesting_fact: The poem's seven short verses each describe one day's finds on a beach - a boot, a spar, seaweed, a fish, driftwood - ending on Sunday's line 'I sit on a rock and I forget/ Sundays and Fridays.' Jaekel chose the poem after realising the building's seven arched windows matched its seven verses exactly, letting passers-by read one line of poetry at a time on their way past rather than all at once. The work was shortlisted for the 2013 Adrian Henri Prize for Poetry in Art and the 2014 Association of Illustrators Awards.

title: Rose Street's Last Original Block
about_site_text: A long run of matching three-storey-and-attic buildings on the south side of Rose Street, put up around 1790 as plain coursed-rubble tenements with small shops let in at street level from early on. Historic Environment Scotland lists the group - numbers 172 to 202 - together as a single Category B entry, describing it as 'a significant surviving part of the original fabric of Edinburgh's New Town.' Shopfronts have been renewed many times since - plate-glass windows, slender columns, modern fascias - but the upper storeys and roofline above still read as unaltered Georgian building fabric.
interesting_fact: Historic Environment Scotland's own listing goes further, calling this specifically the 'last surviving continuous block in Rose Street' - meaning that of all the plain vernacular housing built along the street under Craig's original plan, this run is the only stretch left standing unbroken end to end. Everywhere else on Rose Street, individual buildings have been replaced or rebuilt piecemeal across two and a half centuries of shop-and-pub trading; only here does the original terraced rhythm survive intact - a fixed point on a street otherwise defined by constant turnover.

title: Rose Street's First Pedestrianised Stretch
address: Rose Street at Castle Street, Edinburgh
about_site_text: The block of Rose Street between here at Castle Street and Frederick Street, one block on, holds a small piece of Edinburgh planning history: in 1973 it became the first street in the city closed to traffic and paved for pedestrians only, years ahead of Rose Street's other blocks or Princes Street itself. The new paving came with its own decoration - in the 1980s, artist Maggy Howarth set eight large circular pebble mosaics into the pedestrianised surface at its side-street junctions, each a different rose design worked entirely from small stones, built sturdy enough to carry delivery vans.
interesting_fact: The mosaics haven't all survived intact. Of the original eight, only five remained by the late 2010s, two of them damaged, and Edinburgh Council lifted at least one after it became a pedestrian trip hazard - with talk since of community-led restoration and possible new siting nearby, though their fate is still unresolved as of the most recent reporting found. Look down as well as at the shopfronts through here: what reads as ordinary paving is, in places, four-decade-old public art hanging on by a thread.

title: McVitie's Original Shop
about_site_text: An unremarkable shopfront on Rose Street was, in 1830, the site of a modest provision shop - the first premises of what became McVitie's, now one of Britain's best-known biscuit makers. Robert McVitie ran the business from here, baking and selling bread and confectionery to Rose Street's working trade decades before the family name became a household word. The firm passed down through generations of McVities, expanding well beyond a single shop long before it needed a dedicated factory.
interesting_fact: The digestive biscuit that made the name famous wasn't invented here - that came in 1892, devised by works manager Alexander Grant after the firm had outgrown Rose Street and built its own St Andrews Biscuit Works in Gorgie. Grant's recipe is still the one used today, guarded as a trade secret for well over a century, and the same works later gave the world the Jaffa Cake. The whole enterprise - now sold across dozens of countries - began in this single Rose Street shop, one workshop among many that gave the street its tradesman's character in the shadow of George Street's banks.

title: The Kenilworth
about_site_text: A late-Victorian pub interior behind an unassuming Rose Street frontage, giving little hint of the ornate room inside. The building dates to around 1780, one of Rose Street's original plots, but the interior seen today is the work of architect Thomas Purves Marwick, fitted out in 1899 and trading as the Kenilworth by 1904, named for Sir Walter Scott's 1821 novel. Blue-and-white Minton tiles run floor-to-ceiling under brown-and-white banding, below a patterned red-and-cream plasterwork ceiling, with a Jacobean-revival timber gantry behind the bar. It is Category A listed - Rose Street's highest heritage grade.
interesting_fact: A costly 1966 refit for the old Alloa Brewery, by architects Covell Matthews, restored the pub rather than modernised it - damaged tiling was remade in majolica so closely matched to the originals that today it takes an expert eye to tell 1899 from 1966. The result is one of the best-preserved Victorian pub interiors left in Edinburgh, on a street where most historic bars have long since been stripped out. Scott supplies the theme at one remove: further along Rose Street stands the Abbotsford, named after the house Scott built himself - two pubs, one novelist, one street.

title: Alexander Graham Bell Birthplace
about_site_text: Born here on 3 March 1847, Alexander Graham Bell spent his first years in this New Town flat before the family later moved to the edge of the city. His father, Alexander Melville Bell, was a renowned elocutionist who ran a school from here training teachers of the deaf using his own 'Visible Speech' system - work the young Bell grew up around, and would later echo in Boston. Both his mother and, eventually, his wife were deaf, a thread that ran through his life long before the invention that made him famous.
interesting_fact: Bell left Edinburgh for good in 1870, aged 23, first for Canada and then the United States, where he opened his own school for deaf children in Boston - consciously modelled on his father's Edinburgh work - before patenting the telephone in 1876. A carved stone plaque beside the green door at No.14 still reads simply: 'Alexander Graham Bell, Inventor of the Telephone, Born here 3rd March 1847.'

title: St John's Episcopal Church
address: St John's Church, Princes Street, Edinburgh EH2 4BJ
about_site_text: A Gothic Revival church at the corner of Princes Street and Lothian Road, marking the western gateway into Princes Street Gardens. Architect William Burn was only 25 when he designed it; building began in 1816 and it was dedicated as St John's Chapel on Maundy Thursday 1818. Its plaster fan-vaulted ceiling, modelled on the Henry VII Chapel at Westminster Abbey, is the single most striking feature inside. An Act of Parliament passed the same year construction began banned any further building on the north side of Princes Street, specifically to protect views of the Castle.
interesting_fact: Dean Edward Bannerman Ramsay led the congregation from 1830 to 1872 and became one of Victorian Edinburgh's best-loved churchmen; a granite Celtic cross by Robert Rowand Anderson commemorates him on the Princes Street frontage. The kirkyard holds Anne Rutherford, Sir Walter Scott's mother, alongside Daniel Rutherford, the chemist who discovered nitrogen and was Scott's own uncle. In 2002 a tabot - a sacred replica of the Tablets of the Law used in Ethiopian Orthodox worship - turned up among the church's possessions and was quietly returned to Addis Ababa.

title: St Cuthbert's Parish Church
about_site_text: Tucked into its own churchyard just below St John's, on ground worshipped continuously for longer than almost anywhere else in Edinburgh. Tradition holds that St Cuthbert founded a church here around AD 670, and the site is first documented in a charter of about 1127, when King David I granted St Cuthbert's all the land below the Castle rock. The current building, opened in 1894 to a design by Hippolyte Blanc, is only the latest in a long line on this spot - when the previous Georgian church of 1775 was itself demolished, evidence of six earlier buildings beneath it was reportedly found.
interesting_fact: One thing did survive the 1894 rebuild: the elegant steeple added in 1789-90 by Alexander Stevens, kept standing throughout because it was better built and better looking than the shallow-pitched Georgian roof it once topped. The sprawling graveyard was a favoured target for Burke-and-Hare-era body-snatchers supplying the city's anatomy schools, and watchtowers were built into its boundary walls to guard against them. Buried here: essayist Thomas De Quincey, logarithms inventor John Napier, and William Macao, reckoned the first naturalised Chinese citizen in Scotland.

title: Ross Fountain
address: West Princes Street Gardens, Edinburgh EH1 2EU
about_site_text: A three-tiered cast-iron fountain in ornate French Second Empire style, its nude and semi-nude figures an unlikely sight beneath Edinburgh Castle's ramparts. It was cast at the Durenne foundry in Sommevoire, France, and shown at the 1862 International Exhibition in South Kensington, where Edinburgh gunmaker Daniel Ross bought it for 2,000 pounds and gave it to the city. Shipped north to Leith in 122 separate pieces, it was bolted back together and installed here in West Princes Street Gardens in 1872, close to where the terrace path climbs toward Castle Street.
interesting_fact: The water was switched off in 2008 as the ironwork corroded, and the fountain stood dry for almost a decade until a 1.9 million pound restoration - funded by the Ross Development Trust and carried out by conservators Lost Art Limited - reinaugurated it on 8 July 2018 in a fresh coat of turquoise, brown and gold expected to last around twenty years. Victorian Edinburgh was reportedly uneasy about the figures' undress when it first went up in 1872; some nineteenth-century guidebooks tiptoed around describing them too closely.

title: Norwegian Memorial Stone
address: West Princes Street Gardens (terrace path near Castle Street), Edinburgh EH2 3AA
about_site_text: A weathered grey boulder of Norwegian gneiss, propped on three smaller stones of the same rock and carved with a single inscription, standing quietly on the terrace path a short walk from the Wojtek memorial. It was presented to Edinburgh on 18 September 1978 by veterans of the Norwegian Brigade, the exiled force raised and trained in Scotland during the Second World War after Norway fell to German occupation in 1940. General Sir Roland Gibbs accepted it on behalf of the British Army, asking the Lord Provost to take the stone into the city's care.
interesting_fact: The inscription reads simply: 'During the war years 1940-45 the Norwegian Brigade and other army units were raised and trained in Scotland where we found hospitality, friendship and hope during dark years of exile.' It's an unusual kind of monument - raised not to Scots by outsiders, but by outsiders thanking Scots - and an easy one to walk straight past. It sits within sight of a bear who served in a different exiled army raised in Scotland during the very same war: Wojtek, of the Polish 2nd Corps, memorialised a few dozen metres away.

title: Scottish American War Memorial
address: West Princes Street Gardens (near Castle Street), Edinburgh EH2 3AP
about_site_text: A bronze kilted infantryman kneels on a granite plinth gazing toward Castle Rock, backed by a bronze frieze of soldiers marching off behind a piper. Titled 'The Call 1914', it was sculpted by Robert Tait McKenzie, a Scottish-Canadian based at the University of Pennsylvania, and took him around four years to complete; the figures were cast at the Roman Bronze Works in Brooklyn before shipping to Scotland. Reginald Fairlie was the architect and Colin Macandrew & Partners the builders. It was unveiled on 7 September 1927 by the American Ambassador, Alanson B. Houghton.
interesting_fact: The memorial was a direct gift 'from men and women of Scottish blood and sympathies in the United States of America to Scotland', funded entirely by Scottish-American donors rather than any government, to honour Scots who answered the call to arms in the First World War - the inscription still carries that dedication word for word. The frieze behind the soldier shows ordinary civilians falling into step behind a piper as they turn into recruits, a visual telling of exactly what the title describes. It stands close enough to Wojtek's own memorial that both can be seen from the same stretch of path.

title: Wojtek the Soldier Bear Memorial
address: West Princes Street Gardens, Edinburgh (near Castle Street terrace path)
about_site_text: Unveiled on 7 November 2015, the memorial is the work of Scottish sculptor Alan Beattie Herriot and was cast at Powderhall Bronze in Edinburgh. A bronze soldier of the 2nd Polish Corps walks beside Wojtek at one-and-a-quarter life size, one hand resting on the bear's back. Behind them a low curved granite wall carries a four-metre bronze relief panel tracing Wojtek's wartime journey. It sits on the terrace path in West Princes Street Gardens, below the castle rock near Castle Street. Wojtek was a Syrian brown bear cub, bought from a boy in Iran in 1942 by Polish soldiers on their way to the war. He grew up inside the 22nd Artillery Supply Company, drinking beer, wrestling the men and eating cigarettes.
interesting_fact: Barred from British troopships as a pet, Wojtek was formally enlisted with a paybook and the service number 253. At Monte Cassino in 1944 he is said to have carried crates of artillery shells. He was demobbed in Scotland and died at Edinburgh Zoo in 1963. The granite the pair stand on was quarried at Strzegom in Poland and shipped to Edinburgh, so that the soldier and his bear would always have a piece of their homeland underfoot.

title: Ross Bandstand
about_site_text: An open-air concert venue in a natural bowl of West Princes Street Gardens, directly below Edinburgh Castle. The current structure, officially the Ross Open Air Theatre, was built in 1935 to a design by city architect E. J. Macrae, replacing an earlier bandstand of 1877 that had been gifted by William Henry Ross, chairman of the Distillers Company. It seats around 2,500 and has hosted the Edinburgh International Festival and Edinburgh Jazz Festival for decades, plus the annual Hogmanay concert and the Festival fireworks concert.
interesting_fact: For nearly two decades this stage was also a battlefield of a different kind. From 2004, storm damage and an ambitious £25 million replacement scheme, nicknamed "the Hobbit House" in the press for its curved, grassed canopy roof, dragged through design competitions, hotelier-backed sponsorship deals and public objections over commercialising a free public park. US firm wHY won the international competition in 2017, but the scheme collapsed in 2021 when its main funder pulled out - so the 1935 bandstand still standing here is the one the fight never quite managed to replace.

title: Royal Scots Greys Monument
address: Princes Street, opposite Frederick Street, Edinburgh
about_site_text: A bronze cavalryman of the Royal Scots Greys sits on horseback atop a rough-hewn rock pedestal above the gardens, facing Edinburgh Castle across the valley. Sculpted by William Birnie Rhind with Alessandro Parlanti between 1903 and 1906 and unveiled by Lord Rosebery in 1906, it commemorates the regiment's dead from the Second Boer War of 1899-1902. The soldier wears the exact uniform and equipment the Greys carried to South Africa in 1899, down to the bearskin cap.
interesting_fact: Both the man and the horse are portraits, not composites. The rider was modelled on real Sergeant-Major Anthony James Hinnigan, and the horse beneath him is Polly, who genuinely served with the regiment in South Africa and was cast from life. Plaques added after both World Wars later extended the memorial to the regiment's dead from those conflicts too, so a monument raised for one war ended up carrying the names of three.

title: The Mound
about_site_text: The sloped road you're crossing between West and East Princes Street Gardens isn't natural ground, it's spoil. Constructed in stages between the 1780s and about 1830, an estimated 1.5 million cartloads of earth and rubble dug from the foundations of the New Town were tipped here into the drained bed of the old Nor Loch, gradually building a shortcut between the medieval Old Town and the new Georgian streets above. It was macadamised and landscaped by 1830 and today carries the Royal Scottish Academy and the Scottish National Gallery on its slopes.
interesting_fact: Locals called the original crossing "Geordie Boyd's Brig", after an Old Town clothier named George Boyd who, around 1780, started laying wooden planks across a tip of rubble simply so he could walk over and see the new streets being built. The town council only turned his shortcut into an official project two years later, decreeing in 1782 that all New Town excavation spoil be dumped there systematically. And in 1959, engineers laid an experimental "electric blanket" heating system beneath the road surface to melt winter ice - long disused, but still down there under everyone's feet.

title: Allan Ramsay Monument
address: West Princes Street Gardens, foot of the Mound, Edinburgh
about_site_text: A white Carrara marble statue of the poet and bookseller Allan Ramsay (1686-1758), carved by Sir John Steell and unveiled on 25 March 1865, standing on a pedestal designed by architect David Bryce. Ramsay is shown holding a book in one hand and a pencil in the other, wearing a soft cap rather than the powdered wig fashionable in his day. Medallion portraits of his family and descendants, including his painter son Allan Ramsay the Younger, decorate the sides of the pedestal.
interesting_fact: The cap is a quiet joke about his first career. Before he became a leading figure of the early Edinburgh Enlightenment - founder of one of Britain's first circulating libraries and author of the pastoral comedy "The Gentle Shepherd" - Ramsay trained and worked as a wigmaker, and Steell dressed him in his own nightcap rather than the wig he'd once have sold his customers. The statue was commissioned by Lord Murray of Henderland in memory of his great-uncle.

title: Gardener's Cottage
address: Princes Street Gardens (foot of the Mound), Edinburgh EH2 2HG
about_site_text: Built in 1886 to a design by city architect Robert Morham as the on-site home of the gardens' Head Gardener, this asymmetrical, gabled cottage is built from squared and snecked bull-faced red sandstone under broad eaves with green-painted decorative barge-boarding. Category C listed since 1985, it sits right where the Gardens' two halves meet at the foot of the Mound. No one has lived here for years - the interior was refurbished with period furniture and antiques in 2017, and the cottage now serves as campaign base for the Quaich Project, a partnership between the Ross Development Trust and the City of Edinburgh Council.
interesting_fact: Sources can't even agree which half of the Gardens it belongs to - some call it West Princes Street Gardens, others East - a genuine reflection of how close it sits to the Mound's dividing line. Its most unexpected claim to fame: fans of the CBeebies children's series Tea Cup Travels (2014-2016) will recognise its exterior as Great Aunt Lizzie's cottage, though the interior scenes were filmed elsewhere.

title: Floral Clock
address: West Princes Street Gardens, foot of the Mound, Edinburgh
about_site_text: A working clock made entirely of bedding plants, first switched on 10 June 1903, the earliest floral clock in Britain and among the first anywhere in the world. City parks superintendent John McHattie designed the planting with advice from James Mossman, a descendant of Mary Queen of Scots' court jeweller, while Edinburgh clockmakers James Ritchie & Son built the actual mechanism hidden beneath the flowerbed. It started with only an hour hand; a minute hand followed in 1904.
interesting_fact: A mechanical cuckoo has popped out of a little house beside the clock to sound the quarter-hours since 1953, and the whole bed is dug up and replanted from scratch every single year around a new theme, past years have marked everything from royal jubilees to the centenary of the Flying Scotsman steam locomotive. The original clockwork drive ran until 1973, when it was finally converted to electric power, and thousands of individual plants go into the display each spring to keep the hands moving on time.

title: Royal Scottish Academy Building
about_site_text: A Greek Doric temple front designed by William Henry Playfair and built 1822-26 as the Royal Institution, home in turn to the Royal Society of Edinburgh and the Board of Manufactures before the Royal Scottish Academy took permanent occupancy in 1911. Its foundations needed roughly 2,000 timber piles driven into the soft ground of the old Nor Loch bed before Playfair could build on it at all. Sir John Steell added the rooftop sculpture and the corner sphinxes; the building still hosts rotating exhibitions today, including the RSA's own annual show.
interesting_fact: The figure crowning the pediment is often assumed to be a symbol of wisdom, but it's actually Queen Victoria posed as Britannia, sculpted by Steell not long after she came to the throne. A £32 million underground project completed in the 2010s, the Playfair Project, finally linked this building to its neighbour, the Scottish National Gallery, by a tunnel beneath the Mound, meaning the two Playfair buildings that had stood side by side for close to two centuries were only physically joined within living memory.

title: John Wilson Statue
about_site_text: A bronze of Professor John Wilson (1785-1854), shown in a thoughtful pose holding a half-open manuscript and a quill pen. Sculpted by Sir John Steell and unveiled on 25 March 1865, the same day as the nearby Allan Ramsay statue. Wilson held the Chair of Moral Philosophy at Edinburgh University from 1820 to 1851, but is remembered at least as much for his other life as "Christopher North", the swaggering, pseudonymous voice of the Tory literary journal Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine.
interesting_fact: His appointment to the philosophy chair was a political stitch-up rather than an academic one: Sir William Hamilton was privately reckoned the best-qualified candidate in Britain, but Edinburgh's Tory-run town council pushed Wilson through instead, with Sir Walter Scott leading the campaign for him. He more than made up for it in sheer output - in 1834 alone he wrote over fifty articles for Blackwood's - and as Christopher North he co-created "Noctes Ambrosianae", a long-running series of fictional tavern conversations mixing literary criticism with drinking talk, featuring a character based on his friend the poet James Hogg.

title: Scottish National Gallery
about_site_text: Scotland's national collection of Old Master and Scottish paintings, in a neoclassical building designed by William Henry Playfair. Prince Albert laid the foundation stone on 30 August 1850, calling it in his speech a "temple erected to the Fine Arts", and it opened to the public in 1859. It stands immediately south of Playfair's earlier Royal Scottish Academy building on the same ridge, the two structures forming a matched pair astride the Mound.
interesting_fact: Playfair's original, more ambitious design for the site was rejected as too expensive, and what got built is a scaled-down version, yet even that came with an eccentric extra: plans made public in 2025 for the gallery's 175th anniversary show Victorian engineers had drawn up proposals for a swimming bath in the basement, which was never built. The gallery's Weston Link, opened underground in 2019 as part of the £32 million Playfair Project, now connects it directly to the Royal Scottish Academy next door and down into the gardens below.

title: Playfair Steps
about_site_text: A broad flight of stone steps dropping from Market Street, at the top of the Mound, down to the wide paved forecourt between the Royal Scottish Academy and the Scottish National Gallery. Built around 1828, they're named after William Henry Playfair, architect of both galleries and much else in the city, and they form one of the main pedestrian links between the Old Town above and Princes Street Gardens below.
interesting_fact: During the Edinburgh Festival Fringe, these steps and the plaza at their foot turn into one of the city's busiest informal stages, packed with street performers, jugglers and the crowds who stop to watch them, all summer long. The steps were closed for four years during construction work on the adjoining National Galleries site and only reopened to the public in July 2023, a long wait for what is, in normal times, one of the most heavily used staircases in the city.

title: Adam Black Statue
about_site_text: A bronze statue of publisher and politician Adam Black (1784-1874), shown in the robes of Lord Provost of Edinburgh, holding a scroll. Sculpted by John Hutchison and erected in 1877, three years after Black's death. He founded the publishing house A & C Black, brought out the 7th, 8th and 9th editions of the Encyclopaedia Britannica, served two terms as Lord Provost of Edinburgh, and sat as one of the city's MPs in Parliament from 1856 to 1865.
interesting_fact: Black's biggest single business gamble paid off spectacularly: in 1851 his firm paid £27,000, an enormous sum at the time, to buy up the copyright and printing stock of Sir Walter Scott's Waverley novels, then republished them in cheap shilling editions that put Scott's fiction into ordinary readers' hands for the first time and turned a solid profit for A & C Black in the process. He had started out as a humble Edinburgh bookseller's apprentice.

title: David Livingstone Statue
address: East Princes Street Gardens, next to the Scott Monument, Edinburgh
about_site_text: A bronze of the explorer and missionary David Livingstone (1813-1873), shown mid-stride in a cloak, a Bible in one hand and a lion skin draped at his side. Sculpted by Amelia Robertson Hill and unveiled on 15 August 1876, just three years after Livingstone's death in what is now Zambia. The lion skin recalls an 1844 mauling in which a lion crushed his arm and shoulder, an injury that left him unable to raise that arm fully overhead for the rest of his life.
interesting_fact: The sculptor was a rarity for her era: Amelia Robertson Hill exhibited more than sixty works at the Royal Scottish Academy over her career, yet was barred from full RSA membership purely for being a woman, so in 1877 she helped found Edinburgh's Albert Institute of Fine Arts as an exhibiting society that didn't discriminate by gender. She has a second, closer connection to this walk too: Hill also sculpted three of the figures decorating the Scott Monument, just a few steps from where this statue now stands. Its listing was upgraded from Category B to full Category A in 2002.

title: The Scott Monument
about_site_text: A Victorian Gothic spire of pale Binny sandstone, built 1840-44 and standing 61.1 metres tall. Visitors can climb 287 steps through four viewing platforms to look out over the city. Around its base and up its sides sit 68 carved statuettes of characters from Scott's novels, and a white marble statue of Sir Walter Scott himself by John Steell. Its architect wasn't a trained architect at all. George Meikle Kemp was a self-taught joiner and draughtsman who entered the 1836 design competition under the pseudonym 'John Morvo' - the name of Melrose Abbey's medieval master mason - expecting his lack of credentials to sink his chances.
interesting_fact: He won, but never saw it finished: walking home from the site on a foggy night in March 1844, he fell into the Union Canal and drowned. The monument's famous black colour isn't the stone's own - Binny sandstone is naturally pale. A century and a half of coal smoke from 'Auld Reekie' is what turned it dark.

title: Castle View
address: West Princes Street Gardens, near Ross Bandstand, Edinburgh
about_site_text: From the floor of West Princes Street Gardens, the classic upward view of Edinburgh Castle: a fortress balanced on a sheer volcanic crag rising straight out of what is now manicured parkland. Castle Rock is the neck of an extinct volcano, hard dolerite formed roughly 340 million years ago in the Carboniferous period. Glaciers later ground west to east across the landscape, scouring away the softer surrounding rock on every side except the sheltered eastern flank - leaving the classic 'crag and tail' shape still visible today: the sheer cliff facing this viewpoint, and the long gentle slope of the Royal Mile trailing away behind the fortress on the far side.
interesting_fact: The lawn underfoot used to be underwater. King James III had this natural hollow flooded around 1460 to create the Nor Loch, a defensive loch guarding the castle's northern approach - shallow, stagnant, and for centuries the dumping ground and sewer outlet for the Old Town above. Engineer James Jardine drained its western end between 1813 and 1820 to make way for what became Princes Street Gardens, so this entire grassy vantage point once sat several metres underwater.

title: The Johnnie Walker Experience
about_site_text: This corner of Princes Street and Frederick Street now houses one of Scotland's most ambitious pieces of whisky tourism: an eight-storey immersive experience built inside a completely remodelled former department store (the old Binns store), opened to the public on 6 September 2021. Diageo, the drinks giant behind Johnnie Walker, poured £185 million into the project - the single largest investment ever made in Scotch whisky tourism - transforming the historic building into tasting rooms, interactive galleries tracing the brand's 200-year history, and a rooftop bar looking straight across the city to Edinburgh Castle.
interesting_fact: The experience employs around 150 people and was projected to draw more than half a million visitors in its first year alone - a serious bet on whisky tourism as a growth industry, not just a gift shop for tour buses. Every level tells a different part of the brand's story through film, tasting flights and design details drawn from Johnnie Walker's own history, before finishing on a rooftop terrace with one of the best publicly accessible skyline views in the city.

title: Social Bite
about_site_text: This modest café on Rose Street is where the whole Social Bite movement began. In 2012, Josh Littlejohn and Alice Thompson opened it as a coffee shop that gave its profits to good causes - a straightforward idea that turned into something much bigger. Not long after opening, a young man named Peter, who had been selling The Big Issue outside, came in and asked for a job; hiring him convinced the founders to build supported employment for people with experience of homelessness into the heart of the business, rather than treating it as a side project.
interesting_fact: That single Rose Street shop has since grown into a nationwide social enterprise employing over 75 people - many with lived experience of homelessness - and giving away more than 200,000 items of food a year to people in need. Josh Littlejohn was appointed MBE for the work, and Social Bite's profile grew further when actor and activist George Clooney became a high-profile supporter of the cause.

title: Statue of the Royal Regiment of Scotland
address: West Princes Street Gardens, between the amphitheatre and Ross Fountain, Edinburgh
about_site_text: A reclining bronze lion, inspired directly by the Royal Regiment of Scotland's own cap badge, unveiled by King Charles III on 1 July 2026 in West Princes Street Gardens - sited deliberately between the amphitheatre and Ross Fountain, with the Regiment's headquarters at Edinburgh Castle as its backdrop. Sculptor Kenny Hunter cast the lion in six separate sections, each representing one of the six historic Scottish infantry regiments that amalgamated in 2006 to form the modern Royal Regiment of Scotland.
interesting_fact: The unveiling marked the Regiment's 20th anniversary, but its creators were explicit that the statue isn't a war memorial - it's meant as a quieter tribute to everyone who has served, is serving, or will serve in future, with the lion's reflective, contemplative pose chosen deliberately over anything more triumphant or martial.

title: Police Box Cafe
about_site_text: This pastel pink-and-green kiosk on Rose Street is one of Edinburgh's police boxes - miniature one-person police stations that once stood on street corners across the city, now doing a brisk trade in coffee instead of crime-fighting. City architect Ebenezer MacRae designed the model from 1933, giving each box a pediment, pilasters and cast-iron panelling deliberately styled to blend into the New Town's neo-classical streetscape rather than stand out as municipal furniture. An officer on the beat could check in by phone, log a report, or briefly hold someone inside before a van arrived.
interesting_fact: Despite the resemblance, these are not the same design as Doctor Who's TARDIS - that's modelled on London's police box, a different pattern entirely. Sources vary on the exact original total (widely cited figures range from around 85 up to 142 boxes built across the city from 1933), and the count still standing today is equally hard to pin down - many were decommissioned once radios made them obsolete, and in 2014 the police sold off another 14 of their remaining boxes, keeping just one for themselves. Most survivors, like this one, have been sold on and repurposed as coffee kiosks, flower stalls or takeaway hatches - a genuine recurring sight worth spotting elsewhere on this walk and around the city.

title: Duke of Wellington Statue
about_site_text: An equestrian bronze of Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington, seated on his real Waterloo warhorse Copenhagen and gesturing firmly east toward Waterloo Place. Sculpted by Sir John Steell, who won the commission in 1842, it was unveiled on 18 June 1852, the 37th anniversary of the Battle of Waterloo, and stands directly in front of General Register House at the eastern end of Princes Street.
interesting_fact: Wellington himself, then 83 and in his final months, did not attend the unveiling, but surviving veterans of his campaigns turned out for the ceremony. Copenhagen, the horse, was entirely real: Wellington rode him throughout the Waterloo campaign and kept him in retirement afterwards until he died in 1836, aged 28, and was buried with full military honours. In mid-2026 the statue started turning up in the news for an unwanted reason - spotted wearing a traffic cone, copying a decades-old Glasgow tradition around that city's own Wellington statue after Tartan Army fans crowned statues abroad during the World Cup, a trend Edinburgh councillors have publicly called 'undignified'.

title: General Register House
about_site_text: A grand neoclassical building designed by Robert Adam, its foundation stone laid on 27 June 1774 as purpose-built home for Scotland's national archives - reputedly the first building anywhere in Britain or Ireland constructed specifically to store public records. Money ran out repeatedly and it wasn't fully finished until 1834, sixty years after it began. At its heart sits the Adam Dome, a 50-foot-wide rotunda lit only by a central oculus, modelled on Rome's Pantheon.
interesting_fact: Adam worked small carved thistles into the dome's otherwise thoroughly Roman-inspired anthemion frieze, a quiet Scottish signature in an imported classical language. The building still does the job it was built for nearly 250 years later, holding centuries of Scotland's birth, marriage, death and court records, and remains the seat of the Lord Clerk Register and Lord Lyon King of Arms. It was actually judged too small before it was even finished - later architects Robert Reid and Archibald Elliot were called back in to extend it and dig further storage into the basement.

title: The Balmoral Hotel
about_site_text: A red sandstone clock-tower landmark opened on 15 October 1902 as the North British Station Hotel, built directly above Waverley Station by the North British Railway to a design by William Hamilton Beattie. Its tower rises 190 feet, topped with four 13-foot clock dials made by Edinburgh jewellers Hamilton & Inches. Sean Connery renamed it The Balmoral during a major 1991 refurbishment, and Rocco Forte Hotels has owned it since 1997.
interesting_fact: The clock has run three minutes fast since it first started ticking in 1902, a deliberate trick to help travellers dashing for their train actually catch it - it's only ever set right once a year, at midnight on Hogmanay. J.K. Rowling finished writing Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows in room 552 here on 11 January 2007, later signing a marble bust in the room with the date and a line from the book. The hotel became the first in Scotland to earn a five-star Forbes Travel Guide rating, and past guests have ranged from Laurel and Hardy in 1932 to Oprah Winfrey in 2010.

title: Waverley Bridge
about_site_text: A wide iron-and-stone bridge built 1894-96 by engineers Blyth and Westland, carrying traffic across the deep valley between Princes Street and Market Street/Cockburn Street below - effectively forming the roof of Edinburgh Waverley station underneath it. Category A listed since 1991, it's one of three parallel crossings of this old loch-bed valley, alongside North Bridge and the Mound. Two carriageway ramps once let cars and taxis descend straight into the station concourse; that vehicle access was closed off in January 2014, leaving the ramps to pedestrians, cyclists and deliveries.
interesting_fact: Halfway across the bridge sits the station's former parcels office, itself Category A listed, converted into a pub and restaurant back in the 1980s - so crossing this bridge today can include stopping for a pint directly above the trains rumbling through the station underneath.

title: Edinburgh Waverley Station
about_site_text: Scotland's second-busiest railway station, formed in the 1860s when the North British Railway merged three separate rival Victorian stations that had grown up in this valley since 1846: the North Bridge, General and Canal Street stations. The combined name 'Waverley' had already been used informally from around 1854, borrowed from Sir Walter Scott's Waverley novels. Twenty platforms now radiate from a huge central island beneath a great glass roof, most recently reglazed with 370,000 square feet of clear panels between 2010 and 2012.
interesting_fact: A legal covenant dating back to the station's construction bans any building upward on the site, specifically to protect the view of Arthur's Seat from Princes Street above - one reason Waverley has always had to spread sideways and down into the valley rather than up, squeezed as it is between the Old and New Towns. Because it sits down in that valley, the station is almost entirely hidden from street level, with separate entrances dropping in from Waverley Bridge, Market Street and Princes Street on three different sides of the surrounding city blocks.

title: Waverley Market
about_site_text: A sunken plaza and shopping centre on the site of a Victorian fruit and vegetable market moved here in 1869 after the original marketplace under North Bridge was swallowed up by the growing railway. The Victorian market hall, roofed over in 1874 with an iron-and-glass structure and a rooftop garden used for entertainment, closed in November 1972 and was demolished the following year.
