Water was carried down from reservoirs fed by springs in the Pentland Hills, and the West Bow Well became the first stop for the city's water caddies - workers who queued here to fill their kegs before hauling water door to door through the tenements above the Grassmarket. Its square-plan structure carries a semi-circular drinking basin on one face beneath a 19th-century Edinburgh coat of arms, with a smaller ornamental basin and heraldic panel on its other sides.
interesting_fact: The well stopped supplying water in the early 19th century once piped plumbing reached individual buildings, but a small iron door on it still carries its original inscription: 'The West-Bow Well erected by The Town Council 1674. Repaired and Altered by Richardson Brothers Merchants West Bow 1861.'

title: Museum Context
about_site_text: This three-floor shop on Victoria Street is one of the city's best-known officially licensed Harry Potter retailers, packed with wands, house scarves, robes and collectibles across a warren of small rooms. The building itself has a history that suits its current trade: for more than 130 years it housed Robert Cresser's brush shop, a Victorian ironmonger-style store selling brooms, brushes and household wares from floor-to-ceiling wooden fittings and dusty stock boxes. That original Victorian interior survives largely intact behind the modern merchandise, and its cluttered, old-fashioned character is often cited by visitors and Potter fans as an uncanny match for Ollivanders wand shop in Diagon Alley.
interesting_fact: The shop's top floor has a free photo spot with props and house robes, including a mirror etched with the 'Chamber of Secrets' inscription - a nod to the wider theory, encouraged by J.K. Rowling having written much of the early books nearby, that this curving street inspired Diagon Alley itself.

title: The Enchanted Galaxy
about_site_text: The Enchanted Galaxy sits at the top of Victoria Street and, like its rival Museum Context further down the hill, trades on the street's Diagon Alley reputation - but with a name that took three attempts to land. Run by the Gold brothers, the shop originally opened as 'The Boy Wizard', a name Warner Bros objected to for trading too directly on Harry Potter trademarks. A rebrand to 'The Great Wizard' ran into the same problem, and the owners eventually settled on 'The Enchanted Galaxy', blending magical and sci-fi themes broadly enough to sidestep further disputes while still selling largely Potter-themed merchandise alongside Star Wars, Marvel and other franchise collectibles.
interesting_fact: Where Museum Context leans into cramped, cluttered Victorian atmosphere, The Enchanted Galaxy goes the opposite way - reviewers have compared its clean, brightly lit layout to 'an Apple Store', making the two competing shops, barely 150 metres apart, a study in opposite ways of selling the same theme.

title: Bertie's Proper Fish & Chips
about_site_text: Bertie's occupies a genuinely surprising building for a chip shop: a former church. The site had stood empty for a decade, ever since a serious fire gutted its previous occupant, an Indian restaurant called Khushi's, when the Vittoria Group - the Crolla family's Edinburgh restaurant business - spent £3 million converting the old St John's church into a three-floor, 300-seat fish and chip restaurant that opened in 2018. The name honours Alberto 'Bertie' Crolla, the group's founder, and the restaurant now sits just a few streets from its sister restaurant Landy's on North Bridge, both built on the same family's decades-long fish-and-chip tradition in the city.
interesting_fact: The building's church origins are still legible in its bones - tall arched windows and a soaring, three-storey-high interior - giving diners eating double-cooked chips and battered haddock a dining room shaped like a nave.

title: Finnegan's Wake
about_site_text: Finnegan's Wake has been Victoria Street's Irish pub since 1994, when it took over the premises of a live-music venue called the Preservation Hall and kept the tradition of nightly bands going. Its interior is built around a large circular bar with small wood-panelled booths around the edge and a raised corner stage where bands still play live Irish music most nights, alongside sport on the screens and Guinness on tap. Its name borrows directly from James Joyce's famously dense, unfinished-feeling final novel, itself named after an old Irish-American comic ballad about a hod-carrier who wakes up mid-funeral - a fittingly playful, slightly literary joke for a pub sitting almost next door to Bertie's converted church.
interesting_fact: The pub sits at 9B Victoria Street, immediately beside Bertie's Fish & Chips at number 9 - two very different Irish/British institutions sharing practically the same doorway on the street's lower curve.

title: John Kay's Shop
about_site_text: This small green-fronted shop at the top of Victoria Street sells prints, postcards and Scottish artworks and mementos, and takes its name from John Kay (1742-1826), one of Edinburgh's most important social chroniclers. Kay worked as a barber in the Old Town before his sketching hobby overtook his trade; by 1785 he had given up cutting hair to run a print shop of his own in Parliament Close, where he produced and sold etched caricatures of the city's great and ordinary figures alike. Over nearly 900 etchings between 1785 and 1820, he documented everyone from Enlightenment intellectuals to street vendors, most sketched from nothing more than a passing glance, leaving behind one of the richest visual records of Georgian Edinburgh life.
interesting_fact: The modern shop is a separate business (incorporated in 2017) rather than a surviving continuation of Kay's own print shop, which stood roughly half a mile away in Parliament Close - but its stock of prints, maps and Scottish curiosities makes the name a fitting tribute rather than a coincidence.

title: India Buildings
address: India Buildings, Victoria Street, Edinburgh EH1 2EX
about_site_text: This curved, four-storey Scots Baronial office block was built between 1864 and 1866 to designs by architect David Cousin, its grand interior centred on a domed rotunda ringed by balconies. Its name was likely borrowed from a Liverpool office block of the 1830s, itself named by merchants celebrating the end of the East India Company's monopoly on trade with India - making the building a small piece of Victorian commercial branding transplanted to Edinburgh's Old Town. It originally housed serious institutional tenants, including the British Linen Bank and the Scottish Chamber of Agriculture, fitting for a building built to project financial and civic weight on a street otherwise defined by small shops and closes.
interesting_fact: In January 1906, Indian independence activist Pandurang Mahadev Bapat gave a talk here on British rule in India to an Independent Labour Party meeting - a speech that cost him his government scholarship and pushed him toward the radical movements that led him back to India in 1908 as a freedom fighter.

title: George IV Bar
about_site_text: The George IV Bar sits midway along George IV Bridge, the elevated street built in 1829-32 to carry traffic clear over the Cowgate far below, connecting the Old Town's South Side to the New Town. Today it's a traditional Scottish public house known for a genuinely serious whisky selection - over 100 different malts and blends - alongside regular live music, making it a quieter, more locals-oriented counterpart to the tourist-heavy pubs down in the Grassmarket and on Victoria Street just below.
interesting_fact: The bridge the bar sits on required demolishing two older Old Town streets, Old Bank Close and Liberton's Wynd, when it was built - meaning the ground beneath the bar's foundations covers what was once part of a completely different, now-vanished street layout.

title: Augustine United Church
about_site_text: Augustine United Church's congregation traces back to 1802, when Reverend John Aikman founded a church nearby, in what is now the site of the National Museum of Scotland, out of Edinburgh's radical Reformation tradition. The current building on George IV Bridge was built between 1857 and 1861 by architects J J & W H Hay, blending Romanesque, Renaissance and Classical detailing beneath a distinctive projecting central tower long nicknamed the 'bride's-cake' tower for its tiered, ornamental profile, restored in 2005. Named for Augustine of Hippo, the church has kept its founding congregation's progressive, community-facing character, today hosting numerous Christian and community organisations rather than functioning as a conventional single-congregation parish church.
interesting_fact: The congregation's roots lie in one of Edinburgh's most deprived districts, where working families and their livestock once lived crowded beneath the wealthy merchants and academics of the Royal Mile above - a history the church still cites as the root of its long-running social and community engagement.

title: Frankenstein & Bier Keller
about_site_text: This Gothic former church - built in 1859 and originally an Elim Pentecostal church - now houses one of Edinburgh's more theatrically themed bars. Upstairs, the horror-themed main bar leans into its own name with Frankenstein's-monster decor inside a genuinely Gothic stone shell of pointed arches and spires; downstairs, the Bier Keller recreates a Bavarian beer hall complete with long communal wooden benches, a private bar and a live oompah band on regular nights - an entirely different atmosphere one floor below the horror theming above.
interesting_fact: The building sat abandoned for years after the Elim Pentecostal congregation moved on before its current owners took it on, meaning the pointed arches and spires visible today are the real thing - a genuine former place of worship reused as horror-themed nightlife, not a purpose-built pastiche.

title: Edinburgh Sheriff Court
about_site_text: Edinburgh Sheriff Court has a longer institutional history than its current building suggests. Sheriff court business in the city moved through several homes: an 1816 county hall on the corner of Lawnmarket and George IV Bridge, then a purpose-built Renaissance Revival courthouse designed by David Bryce and completed in 1868, before hearings eventually relocated to the Chambers Street building the court occupies today. The office of procurator fiscal that prosecutes cases through this court traces back even further, with the earliest documented references in Scottish records dating to the 1550s - making the basic machinery of local Scottish criminal justice centuries older than any of the buildings that have housed it.
interesting_fact: The Sheriff Court and the adjoining Justice of the Peace Court still share the same ornate iron gateway and postbox-style enquiry point pictured at the entrance, a small formal touch that survives from an era when court buildings were built to visibly project civic authority to everyone passing on the street.

title: Crown Office
about_site_text: The headquarters of the Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service - the body that investigates and prosecutes crime across all of Scotland - occupies a building that started life as a college. Built from 1872-74 to designs by David Rhind (with David Cousin and John Lessels), it was originally the Watt Institution and School of Arts, which in 1885 merged with the centuries-old George Heriot Trust to become Heriot-Watt College, the direct ancestor of today's Heriot-Watt University. Its imposing 268-foot Renaissance-influenced facade, borrowing from French chateau architecture, was designed to give a technical college the civic gravity of a bank or a courthouse - gravity the building has kept ever since, just in service of a different institution.
interesting_fact: Heriot-Watt University's own roots run through this one Chambers Street address before the college eventually outgrew it and moved to its present Riccarton campus, meaning Scotland's chief prosecuting authority now works out of what was, in effect, an early ancestor of a modern Scottish university.

title: William Chambers Monument
about_site_text: This statue honours Sir William Chambers (1800-1883), the publisher-turned-Lord-Provost who reshaped this part of the Old Town more than almost anyone else. He and his brother Robert built a printing and publishing empire from a small Peebles bookshop, but it was as Lord Provost from 1865 that Chambers left his biggest mark: pushing through the 1867 Edinburgh Improvement Act, which cleared entire slum closes and cut new streets - including the one that now bears his name - through some of the city's most overcrowded ground. Sculpted by John Rhind on a plinth by H.J. Blanc, the statue was erected in 1891, originally standing in the middle of Chambers Street itself.
interesting_fact: The statue was moved to its current position in 2016, when the pedestrian area was widened to make room for a second, similarly styled statue directly nearby - William Henry Playfair, the architect whose buildings Chambers Street was built to celebrate.

title: William Henry Playfair Monument
about_site_text: Standing a few steps from the William Chambers monument it deliberately echoes, this statue honours William Henry Playfair (1790-1857), the architect behind more of Edinburgh's best-known buildings than perhaps any other single figure - the National Gallery, the Royal Scottish Academy, the National Monument on Calton Hill and Surgeons' Hall among them. Sculpted by Alexander Stoddart and unveiled in 2016, it deliberately mirrors the style, scale and pose of the older Chambers statue nearby, portraying Playfair in period dress with papers in hand, as though caught mid-design.
interesting_fact: The statue was commissioned specifically to give Playfair - whose neoclassical buildings define huge parts of central Edinburgh's skyline - the same kind of permanent public recognition long since given to Chambers, more than 125 years after the earlier statue went up a few metres away.

title: Hotel du Vin & Bistro
about_site_text: This boutique hotel occupies a cluster of former institutional buildings dating back to 1743, which over the centuries served in turn as a poorhouse, an asylum, and later a science laboratory, before Hotel du Vin restored and connected them into a single luxury hotel. Ten of its rooms sit within the original historic buildings, kept deliberately atmospheric, while a newer wing built onto the site matches them in style. The hotel keeps a whisky snug and a specialist wine-tasting room among its features, alongside its bistro and mezzanine bar, trading on the contrast between the building's institutional past and its now thoroughly comfortable present.
interesting_fact: Guests booking the hotel's older rooms are, in effect, staying inside a converted 18th-century asylum - one of several former asylums and poorhouses across Edinburgh's Old Town that have been repurposed for hospitality rather than demolished.

title: The Gilded Saloon
about_site_text: The Gilded Saloon opened in July 2025 as a joint venture between the Gilded Balloon, Paradise Palms and Kelburn Arts, but its name carries real weight in Edinburgh's comedy and arts scene: it's a direct tribute to the original Gilded Saloon, a beloved Cowgate performance bar destroyed in the catastrophic Cowgate fire of December 2002, which also burned down the entire Gilded Balloon venue and ten other Old Town businesses. The new bar, restaurant and 200-capacity performance venue overlooking Bristo Square revives the name more than two decades on, serving craft beer and pub food from local chef Tomas Gormley alongside a full comedy and arts programme.
interesting_fact: The original Gilded Saloon had itself replaced an earlier venue, the 369 Gallery, when that closed in the late 1990s - meaning the current bar carries the memory of a lineage of Cowgate arts venues stretching back decades, not just its immediate 2002-destroyed predecessor.

title: Doctors
about_site_text: This corner building has been serving Forrest Road since 1874, built specifically to house small businesses connected to the old Royal Infirmary, which then stood almost directly opposite. Its two longest-standing tenants both served that hospital trade directly: George Watson, a cabinet and coffin maker, worked from the building from 1884 to 1959, while surgical instrument maker James Gardiner traded there until the early 1960s, eventually closing under pressure from larger manufacturers. After a spell as a barbecue restaurant and then a pub called The Mortar from 1970, the building took on its current name, Doctors, in 1979 - a direct nod to the vanished hospital across the street that had shaped the building's purpose for over a century.
interesting_fact: The pub's name outlived the hospital it referenced by decades - the old Royal Infirmary across the road closed for good when services moved to Little France in 2003, but Doctors, named in its honour, is still trading today.

title: The Kid's Secret Garden
about_site_text: Tucked just off Middle Meadow Walk, this small community garden is run as a free, volunteer-maintained space for local children and families, built from reclaimed timber into benches, planters and a hand-painted sign rather than any formal civic design. It sits at the point where Middle Meadow Walk - the tree-lined path laid out from 1722 on the drained bed of the old Burgh Loch - opens out toward the Meadows themselves, making it a genuinely grassroots addition to one of Edinburgh's oldest planned green routes rather than part of its original historic design.
interesting_fact: Spaces like this - informal, community-built gardens tucked into gaps beside major paths - have become increasingly common across Edinburgh's Old and New Towns as local groups reclaim small unused plots of land, and this one is a good example of that wider, very recent trend sitting right alongside 300-year-old infrastructure.

title: Edinburgh Futures Institute
about_site_text: This grand Scots Baronial building, completed in 1879 to designs by David Bryce, was originally the Old Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh - considered, in its day, one of the best-planned hospitals in Britain, with ward pavilions spaced apart for fresh air and reduced cross-infection, set deliberately next to the Meadows for patients recovering. It served as Edinburgh's main hospital until services moved to a new site at Little France in 2003, after which the category-A-listed building sat effectively unused for years before the University of Edinburgh undertook a seven-year, multi-million-pound restoration, reopening it in June 2024 as the Edinburgh Futures Institute - a 20,000 square metre home for interdisciplinary research, teaching and business incubation.
interesting_fact: The building's distinctive clock tower, visible for miles across the city, has stood watch over this stretch of Lauriston Place through more than 140 years and two completely different institutional lives - as one of Britain's most advanced Victorian hospitals, and now as a 21st-century university research hub.

title: Simpson Loan
about_site_text: Simpson Loan is one of the main streets running through Quartermile, the large residential and office redevelopment of the former Old Royal Infirmary site, mixing sleek modern glass apartment blocks with the restored Victorian hospital buildings around them. Its name honours Sir James Young Simpson, the Edinburgh professor of midwifery who first demonstrated the anaesthetic properties of chloroform in 1847 and introduced it into obstetric and surgical practice right here at the Royal Infirmary that once stood on this ground - making the street name a direct link between the site's medical history and the development built on top of it.
interesting_fact: Quartermile's street names throughout the development consistently reference figures connected to the old hospital's medical history, of which Simpson Loan is one of the most prominent examples - a rare case of new-build street naming in Edinburgh deliberately preserving a site's institutional memory rather than starting from scratch.

title: Lister Square
about_site_text: Lister Square is the public heart of Quartermile, framed by the glass-and-steel Quartermile One office block and the surrounding cafes and shops of the development. Like Simpson Loan nearby, its name reaches back into the site's medical history: it honours Joseph Lister, the pioneer of antiseptic surgery whose techniques - developed in the era when this site was Edinburgh's Royal Infirmary - dramatically cut post-operative infection rates and made modern surgery survivable worldwide. The square now functions as Quartermile's main public gathering space, hosting outdoor seating, events and a mix of leisure and retail units built into the restored and new buildings around it.
interesting_fact: Lister's name appears twice within a few hundred metres of this square - once here in Lister Square, and again a few streets away in the separate Lister Housing Co-operative on Lauriston Place, which was itself part-funded through a trust set up in his memory.

title: George Heriot's School Turrets
about_site_text: These conical corner turrets are part of George Heriot's School's main quadrangular building, begun in 1628 under master mason William Wallace and completed after his death in 1631. The turrets are a textbook example of a decorative feature that recurs across Edinburgh's grandest historic buildings - originally derived from defensive tower design on castles and tower houses, but adopted purely ornamentally on Renaissance-era civic and institutional buildings like this one to signal status and craftsmanship rather than to serve any defensive purpose. Heriot's own turrets carry ball-finialled lead roofs and, on the chapel turrets specifically, the carved arms of the school's founder, the royal goldsmith George Heriot.
interesting_fact: The same turret style appears on buildings all across the Old and New Town - from tenement stair-towers to grand institutions like this one - making it one of the most immediately recognisable architectural signatures of historic Edinburgh, quite apart from any single building it happens to sit on.

title: Ornate Iron Railings
about_site_text: These spear-topped cast-iron railings, fencing off a sunken basement stairwell on Keir Street, are one of the most common decorative features across Edinburgh's Georgian and Victorian streets. Cast iron became cheap and widely available in Scotland through the 18th and 19th centuries thanks to the country's ironworking industry, and virtually every New Town and tenement-lined Old Town street was fitted with railings like these - both to fence off the sunken 'area' in front of basement windows and doors, and simply to mark property boundaries in an attractive, uniform style. Most surviving examples, this one included, are on category-listed buildings and are protected as part of the character of Edinburgh's UNESCO World Heritage Site.
interesting_fact: During the Second World War, many of Edinburgh's railings were controversially requisitioned and melted down for the war effort - meaning surviving original ironwork like this, rather than post-war replacement railings, is now genuinely valued as a rarer historical survival.

title: Iron Boot Scraper
about_site_text: Set low into the stone stairs beside the railings at 18 Keir Street, this small cast-iron boot scraper is a fixture once found outside almost every Georgian and Victorian townhouse in Edinburgh. Before the city's streets were consistently paved and drained, mud, horse dung and general filth were unavoidable underfoot, and a boot scraper by the front door let residents and visitors clean their soles before stepping inside onto good carpets and floors. Most were cast in one piece with a flat blade for scraping and a small brush-holder or spike beside it, fixed directly into the stonework of the entrance steps - a small, functional detail now mostly obsolete but still visible outside thousands of Old and New Town doorways.
interesting_fact: Boot scrapers are one of the few genuinely functional (rather than purely decorative) pieces of historic street furniture still surviving in large numbers across Edinburgh, precisely because removing them meant chiselling them out of solid stone steps rather than simply unscrewing them.

title: Flower-Decorated Tenement Steps
about_site_text: Residents of this Keir Street tenement have filled their stone entrance steps with dozens of potted plants and flowers, turning a purely functional stairway into one of the street's small highlights. This kind of communal doorstep gardening is a genuinely widespread tradition across Edinburgh's tenement blocks, where residents typically don't have private gardens of their own - stone steps, window ledges and small shared areas in front of stairwells become the only outdoor space available, and many residents' associations and individual flat-owners take real pride in dressing them with planters, hanging baskets and seasonal flowers.
interesting_fact: Tenement stair 'stair pride' displays like this one are common enough across Edinburgh that they've become an informal part of the city's character - the same stone steps that once needed a boot scraper to keep mud off them now often double as makeshift plant stands.

title: Argyle House - 60s architectural eyesore
about_site_text: Argyle House is Edinburgh's most argued-about building - a hulking 1968 concrete-and-harling office block, designed by Michael Laird & Partners, that sits squarely across West Port in the middle of the Old Town's historic skyline. It went up on the site of John Croall & Son, a long-established garage and Rolls-Royce coachbuilder, after the developer Argyle Securities bought the land in 1961. Its route to approval ran through the city's 1953 Development Plan, which had rezoned the then-decaying West Port and High Riggs area for commercial use - quietly making land that had only ever supported housing suddenly valuable for large-scale office development. The Corporation Planning Committee approved the scheme in September 1966, in a decade when postwar modernisation was consistently prioritised over conservation concerns across British cities, Edinburgh included.
interesting_fact: Even architecture critics sympathetic to the building struggled to defend it - Colin McWilliam tried comparing its scale to Georgian terraces, but still admitted it was 'preposterously large and a potential rival to the Castle rock.' No public opposition to the scheme survives in the historical record, a telling contrast to how fiercely similar proposals are fought today.

title: 6VT Edinburgh City Youth Cafe
about_site_text: 6VT is a charitable youth cafe serving young people across Edinburgh from ages 0 to 26, tucked into the foot of the Vennel just below its famous view up to the Castle. Rather than a formal community centre, it operates as a genuine drop-in space - open several evenings a week alongside structured group work, one-to-one support and links to wider services - built specifically so young people have somewhere informal to connect, try new things and get help without it feeling institutional. The name '6VT' comes directly from its address, and the cafe has become a fixture of this stretch of the Old Town, sitting just metres from the historic Flodden Wall remnant the Vennel is famous for.
interesting_fact: The cafe occupies a genuinely tiny footprint for the range of services it runs, relying on the surrounding stonework of the old Flodden and Telfer Walls as part of its own boundary - a modern youth charity operating literally within a 16th-century defensive wall.

title: Brown's Place
about_site_text: This quiet residential square opening off the Vennel takes its name from James Brown, who ran an inn next door in the Grassmarket. When the Flodden Wall - which had marked the edge of the city here since 1513 - was gradually demolished after 1815, following the Union and Napoleon's defeat removed any remaining need for city defences, Brown seized the chance to develop the land behind his inn, very likely reusing stone salvaged from the wall itself. By 1834 the square was being advertised as 'newly built.' It survived a serious threat in the 1960s, when numbers 1-3 stood derelict and the whole area was earmarked for demolition to expand the nearby art college - plans that were ultimately abandoned by decade's end, with those buildings rehabilitated in 1976.
interesting_fact: A residents' association formed in 1986 specifically to restore the square's shared garden, part of which had been concreted over at some point - reclaiming a small green space that Brown himself had built directly on top of the city's old defensive wall.

title: The Black Bull
about_site_text: The Black Bull has traded from this corner of the Grassmarket since at least the early 20th century, part of one of the highest concentrations of historic pubs anywhere in Edinburgh - a market square with written records of trading stretching back to around 1370. Old photographs comparing the pub in 1912 and a century later show the building itself has been rebuilt at some point, even as the pub's name and location have stayed constant. Today it runs as a sports bar with a long L-shaped bar and two small mezzanine levels, decorated with memorabilia from T&J Bernard, one of Edinburgh's several long-vanished local breweries.
interesting_fact: The pub keeps memorabilia from T&J Bernard, a brewery that no longer exists - a small, deliberate way of keeping Edinburgh's lost brewing history visible inside a pub that has itself already survived at least one full rebuild.

title: Victoria Street's Cobbles
about_site_text: The cobbled setts curving down Victoria Street are a genuine survival of a paving technique once universal across Edinburgh's Old Town, laid using roughly cut rectangular granite blocks (properly called 'setts' rather than true rounded cobbles) bedded into sand and gravel. Streets were paved this way from the 18th century onward because granite setts were durable enough to survive horse-drawn cart traffic and could be re-laid individually when damaged, unlike a continuous surface. Most of Edinburgh's other streets have long since been resurfaced in tarmac for modern traffic, making Victoria Street's intact, curving run of setts - still visibly worn smooth by two centuries of footfall and cartwheels - one of the best-preserved and most photographed stretches of historic paving left in the city.
interesting_fact: The double yellow lines painted directly onto the historic setts are a small, constant tension point for conservation bodies - modern traffic regulation applied directly on top of 19th-century stonework, on a street that's otherwise treated as one of Edinburgh's most protected historic assets.

title: Museum on the Mound
about_site_text: This free museum occupies part of the Bank of Scotland's original headquarters, a grand building designed by Robert Reid and Richard Crichton and built between 1802 and 1806 at a cost of £43,000 for a bank that was already, by then, over a century old - founded in 1695 as Scotland's first bank, and in 1696 the first commercial bank in Europe to issue paper banknotes. The museum itself opened in 2006, two years before the global financial crisis it now can't help but be read through, and covers the story of money and banking through historic banknotes (including Scotland's oldest surviving note), an interactive 1820s life-assurance display, exhibits on financial crime and security, and raised maps tracing the Old Town's development since the 1600s.
interesting_fact: The building has never stopped being a working bank headquarters even while housing a museum - it remains the Scottish headquarters of Lloyds Banking Group today, meaning visitors touring 300 years of banking history are doing so inside an active modern bank building, not a retired one.

title: Assembly Hall
about_site_text: This neo-Gothic hall, designed by David Bryce in 1858, sits directly east of Edinburgh Castle atop the Mound and has served since 1929 as the meeting place for the General Assembly of the Church of Scotland - the church's annual governing gathering. It was built for the Free Church of Scotland in the wake of the 1843 Disruption, when a large breakaway movement split from the established Church and urgently needed its own theological college, assembly hall and church nearby. One of its most historically significant moments came in 1910, when 1,355 delegates gathered here for the World Missionary Conference, an event widely credited as the starting point of the modern ecumenical movement. Between 1999 and 2004 it took on an entirely different role, hosting the newly reconvened Scottish Parliament while the purpose-built Holyrood building was under construction.
interesting_fact: Today, for three weeks every August, this same hall housing Scotland's national church assembly transforms into one of the Edinburgh Festival Fringe's most prestigious venues, hosting circus, comedy, music and dance across three separate performance spaces inside it.

title: Edinburgh City Relief Map
about_site_text: Set into the pavement on the Mound, this bronze high-relief model reproduces central Edinburgh in miniature - from Lothian Road in the west to Regent Road in the east, and from Queen Street in the north down to the Cowgate in the south - with the Castle, Calton Hill, Waverley Station and Princes Street Gardens all rendered in raised bronze detail, alongside raised lettering naming the major streets. It was presented to the City of Edinburgh in 1984 by the staff of the Edinburgh branch of Marks & Spencer to mark the company's centenary, but its real purpose is tactile rather than decorative: the whole point of casting the city in high relief was to let visitors with visual impairments explore the shape and grandeur of Edinburgh's skyline entirely by touch.
interesting_fact: Because it's designed to be touched rather than just looked at, decades of hands tracing the Castle Rock, the Mound and the major streets have left the bronze polished to a bright golden sheen in exactly those spots, while the rest of the map has darkened naturally with age - a map that visibly records where people actually explore it most.

title: The Merchants' Hall
about_site_text: The Merchants' Hall is the headquarters of the Company of Merchants of the City of Edinburgh, a body whose roots trace back to the trade guilds of the 13th and 14th centuries, formalised into its modern form by a Royal Charter granted by Charles II in 1681. The current 19th-century building on Hanover Street, a Category B listed structure, was built to project exactly the values the Company still associates itself with - integrity, commercial acumen and civic accomplishment - and its interior includes a genuinely striking Minstrels' Gallery. The Company's influence reaches well beyond this one hall: it still founded and funds two of Edinburgh's best-known independent schools, George Watson's College and Erskine Stewart's Melville, continuing a charitable and educational role that stretches back through the Company's entire 340-plus-year history.
interesting_fact: The Hall runs a permanent exhibition inside chronicling the Company's full history 'from 1681 to the present day' - meaning this working private hall, still used for events and private hire, is also one of Edinburgh's more discreet, lesser-known small museums.

title: Former TSB Bank, Hanover Street
about_site_text: This imposing neo-Greek bank building, a Category A listed structure, was built in 1939 to designs by the architects Oldrieve, Bell and Paterson for the Edinburgh Savings Bank, later absorbed into the TSB network whose name still sits carved above its entrance. Its tetrastyle Ionic portico - four full-height fluted columns across the Hanover Street facade - is built from Darney sandstone on a plinth of light grey Creetown granite, with the substructure masonry by G. and R. Cousin of Edinburgh and the superstructure by Jackson, Brown of Giffnock. Decorative roundels above the flanking entrances carry TSB's own arms, a two-towered castle with a closed portcullis, while the arms of Edinburgh, Leith and Musselburgh appear elsewhere on the facade, marking out the three burghs the bank originally served.
interesting_fact: The building's banking hall was designed on a genuinely double-height scale, built in 1939 to project total financial permanence and trustworthiness right as the Second World War was breaking out - and the site has since been earmarked for conversion into a pub and restaurant, a change of use that will keep the grand banking hall but end its 85-plus years as a working bank.

title: All Bar One, George Street
about_site_text: This grand Georgian corner building at the junction of George Street and Hanover Street was originally constructed as a bank, its scale and formal stone facade - with balustraded upper storeys and heavy classical detailing wrapping both street frontages - built specifically to project financial solidity on one of the New Town's most prominent corners. Like many of Edinburgh's historic bank buildings, it has since been repurposed for hospitality; it now trades as an All Bar One, with the original double-height banking hall giving the modern bar an unusually grand, high-ceilinged interior far larger than a purpose-built pub of the same footprint would ever have.
interesting_fact: The building's position - directly on the crossing of George Street and Hanover Street, two of the New Town's principal axes - meant that whichever bank originally built it was making a deliberate statement of prestige simply through its address, long before anyone had heard of All Bar One.

title: Stone Basements and Area Wells
about_site_text: The sunken stone-walled gap running beneath the railings at 16 Keir Street is a classic Edinburgh 'area' - a below-street-level space in front of a tenement's basement windows and door, built into virtually every Georgian and Victorian terrace in the city. Areas exist because these buildings' ground floors sit slightly raised above street level, with a basement or 'garden flat' beneath; rather than leaving that basement level buried and windowless, builders left a narrow open trench along the front wall, faced in dressed stone and fenced off with railings, so the basement rooms could get proper daylight and their own street-level door. The stone retaining wall and curving stair down to the basement door, visible here beneath the ironwork, are essentially unchanged from when the tenement was first built.
interesting_fact: Areas like this one are the reason Edinburgh's New Town and tenement streets needed so much cast ironwork in the first place - the railings weren't purely decorative, they were essential safety barriers stopping pedestrians from stepping straight down into a basement-level drop hidden right at the edge of the pavement.

title: Radisson Blu Hotel
address: The Royal Mile, 80 High St, Edinburgh EH1 1TH, UK
about_site_text: The turreted, sandstone-fronted Radisson Blu sits on the site of Dickson's Close, a narrow medieval alley recorded from at least 1723 that once ran down to the Cowgate. The close was named after the merchant Thomas Dickson and had earlier been known as Aikman's Close and Halyburton's Close, after successive residents going back to the early 1500s. It was swept away when Niddry Street was widened to build the modern hotel, and today only the old street sign survives, mounted above a doorway on the building.
interesting_fact: One of Dickson's Close's most notable residents was the artist David Allan, nicknamed the 'Scottish Hogarth' for his satirical engravings and illustrations - he's buried across town in Old Calton Burial Ground.

title: Carrubber's Close
about_site_text: Carrubber's Close takes its name from James Hay of Carruber, a 15th-century landowner who held ground and a coal yard here. In 1736 the poet Allan Ramsay converted an old playhouse at the foot of the close into Scotland's first purpose-built theatre, defying strict Presbyterian opposition to stage drama in the city. The building later passed through several religious congregations, becoming known as the Whitefield Chapel after evangelist George Whitefield preached there.
interesting_fact: After the old theatre building was eventually demolished, the site became home to the Carrubbers Christian Mission, whose current hall - funded by American evangelist D.L. Moody in 1883 - still stands in the close today.

title: North Bridge Arcade
address: 7 North Bridge, Arcade, Edinburgh EH1 1QL, UK
about_site_text: The North Bridge Arcade is a covered Victorian shopping arcade built in 1899-1902 to designs by Dunn & Findlay, linking North Bridge with Cockburn Street. It's one of only five surviving arcades of its kind in Scotland, and its centrepiece is a stained-glass rotunda with a gold-and-turquoise mosaic ceiling that gives the space a starlit glow.
interesting_fact: The arcade sits within the building sometimes known as 'The Scotsman Buildings' - the former home of The Scotsman newspaper, just steps from Waverley Station.

title: Bishop's Close
address: 129 High St, Bishop's Cl, Edinburgh EH1 1SG, UK
about_site_text: Bishop's Close is named for Bishop's Land, the grand townhouse of Archbishop John Spottiswood, who died here in 1639, and later home to Bishop Thomas Sydserf. By the 19th century the tenement had filled with ordinary Old Town families, and from the 1880s onward it became home to Jewish families fleeing persecution in Eastern Europe, including the Emmanuel family who had arrived from England in 1841.
interesting_fact: The close sits sandwiched directly between two pubs, The Mitre Bar and the Royal Mile Tavern - The Mitre's very name is a nod to the bishop's headgear, tying the two neighbouring sites together.

title: The Mitre Bar
about_site_text: The Mitre Bar takes its name from the site's earlier history: in 1615 a fine tenement here belonged to Archbishop John Spottiswood, Bishop of St Andrews, and the tavern's name and sign recall his mitre. The original building burned down in 1814 and was rebuilt as the pub that stands today, now part of the Nicholson's collection of historic Edinburgh pubs.
interesting_fact: Local legend holds that the bishop's own throne lies buried beneath the bar - and that his ghost still walks the premises.

title: Bailie Fyfe's Close
about_site_text: Bailie Fyfe's Close is named after Gilbert Fyfe, a merchant and city magistrate (a 'bailie') who lived here between 1677 and 1686. The close stood directly in the path of the Great Fire of Edinburgh, which broke out on the night of 15 November 1824 in an engraver's workshop just around the corner in Old Assembly Close, when an overheated pot of linseed oil set light to a stack of paper.
interesting_fact: The 1824 fire burned for five days, destroyed dozens of buildings across the full width of the Old Town between the High Street and Cowgate, and left over 400 people homeless - one of the worst disasters in the city's history.

title: The Nutcracker Christmas Shop
about_site_text: The Nutcracker is one of the Royal Mile's few shops dedicated entirely to Christmas, open year-round rather than just in December. Its narrow High Street frontage is packed with baubles, tartan decorations, and traditional wooden nutcrackers, drawing browsing tourists past its window displays whatever the season.
interesting_fact: Permanent Christmas shops like this one are a Royal Mile tradition in their own right - Edinburgh's festive trade has become a year-round draw for visitors, not just a winter one.

title: Stevenlaw's Close
about_site_text: Stevenlaw's Close is named after Steven Law, a supporter of Mary Queen of Scots during the civil war of the early 1570s. The narrow close cuts steeply down from the High Street to the Cowgate between high tenement walls, a classic Old Town 'close' - built to pack maximum housing into minimum street frontage.
interesting_fact: One notorious former resident was James 'Daft Jamie' Wilson, a well-known Old Town figure who became one of the victims of the West Port murderers Burke and Hare, who killed to supply cadavers for anatomical dissection.

title: New Assembly Close
about_site_text: New Assembly Close took its name when Edinburgh's fashionable dancing assembly moved here from Old Assembly Close in 1736, remaining until 1784. The building later housed the Edinburgh Assembly Rooms, the King's Arms Tavern, and even the Edinburgh Wax Museum, before the Commercial Bank built its head office on the site in 1814.
interesting_fact: The 18th-century Assembly was run by female managers and often doubled as a charitable fundraiser for the city's hospitals - a rare example of women holding formal organisational control over Edinburgh's high society.

title: Netherbow Wellhead
about_site_text: This carved stone wellhead, designed by Sir William Bruce and built by master mason Robert Mylne in 1675, once supplied some of Old Town Edinburgh's first piped drinking water - carried three miles from the Comiston Springs into storage tanks on Castlehill and out to public wellheads like this one. Its two grotesque bronze masks, one facing east and one west, are replicas of the originals.
interesting_fact: The wellhead fell out of daily use once Victorian housing modernisation brought indoor plumbing to Old Town tenements, but it was restored to working order - with running water again - by the Edinburgh Old Town Renewal Trust in 1997.

title: Old Assembly Close
about_site_text: Old Assembly Close was originally called Little's Close, after the brothers Clement and William Little, before Edinburgh's dancing assembly - which began in 1723 - gave it its present name. The great hall here hosted the city's high society balls until the assembly moved to New Assembly Close in 1736, and the original hall was later destroyed in the Great Fire of 1824, which started in an engraver's workshop in this very close.
interesting_fact: The 1824 fire began when a pot of overheated linseed oil in James Kirkwood's engraving workshop set a stack of paper alight - within hours the flames had spread along the High Street rooftops, fanned by a southwesterly wind.

title: Borthwick's Close
about_site_text: Borthwick's Close is one of the many narrow medieval closes running off the High Street near St Giles' Cathedral and Parliament Square, most named after a resident merchant, tradesman, or landowner whose identity has often been lost to time. Like its neighbours, it was built to squeeze maximum tenement housing into a tight sliver of Old Town street frontage.
interesting_fact: Closes like this one were sealed at night by a locked gate at the street end - hence the name 'close' - a security measure for the crowded, largely self-contained communities living up the shared stairs above.

title: Statue of James Braidwood
about_site_text: This bronze statue in Parliament Square honours James Braidwood (1800-1861), who in 1824 became the first Master of Engines of Edinburgh's fire brigade - the world's first municipal fire service. Braidwood introduced protective helmets and uniforms and pioneered the then-radical idea of training firefighters to enter burning buildings rather than simply spraying water from outside.
interesting_fact: Braidwood later became head of the London Fire Engine Establishment and died fighting a warehouse fire on Tooley Street in 1861, aged 61, when a collapsing wall killed him - the statue was unveiled in 2008, funded by a former Lothian & Borders Firemaster.

title: The Supreme Courts
about_site_text: Behind Parliament Square's facade lies Parliament House, built on the orders of Charles I and completed in 1639 as the seat of the pre-Union Scottish Parliament - the world's first purpose-built parliament building. Since the Union of 1707 it has housed Scotland's supreme courts, the Court of Session and High Court of Justiciary, spread across more than 700 rooms behind the historic frontage.
interesting_fact: Parliament Hall, the oldest part of the complex, has a magnificent hammer-beam oak ceiling and still serves lawyers today as a 'salle des pas perdus' - a hall for pacing and informal conference between court appearances, a tradition unbroken for nearly 200 years.

title: Charles II Statue
about_site_text: This lead equestrian statue of Charles II, erected in 1685 - the year of his death - is believed to be the oldest statue in Edinburgh and possibly the oldest lead equestrian statue in Britain. It depicts the king in Roman military dress, carrying a baton as a symbol of imperial authority, on a pedestal carved from Craigleith stone by Robert Mylne, the King's Master Mason.
interesting_fact: Charles II's own path to the throne ran through Edinburgh: after his father's execution in 1649, the Scottish Parliament proclaimed him king, but Cromwell crushed his forces at the Battle of Worcester in 1651, forcing him into exile until the monarchy's restoration in 1660.

title: Roxburgh's Close
about_site_text: Roxburgh's Close is thought to take its name from John Roxburgh, a chef recorded living here in 1635. Like many Old Town closes it fell out of everyday use for long stretches as surrounding buildings changed hands and function, before being reopened as part of later redevelopment of the Royal Mile's historic street pattern.
interesting_fact: The closes running off the Royal Mile were never simple back alleys - each was effectively its own tiny neighbourhood, with tenement stairs holding dozens of households stacked above shops and workshops at street level.

title: Bank of Scotland
address: Bank of Scotland Private Banking, The Mound, Edinburgh EH1 1YZ, UK
about_site_text: Bank of Scotland's headquarters has crowned the top of the Mound since 1806, when architects Robert Reid and Richard Crichton - both former pupils of Robert Adam - completed a domed Georgian villa on land the bank bought from the city in 1800. David Bryce substantially enlarged the building in 1862, adding the grand central dome and domed wings that give the skyline its present silhouette.
interesting_fact: Founded in 1695, Bank of Scotland is one of the oldest banks in the world still trading under its original name, and its Mound headquarters remains the registered Scottish office of Lloyds Banking Group today.

title: Wardrop's Court
address: Wardrop Court, Lawnmarket, Edinburgh EH1 2NY, UK
about_site_text: Wardrop's Court was formed behind the Lawnmarket in the 1890s, on the site of the older Middle Baxter's Close, after a wave of tenement demolition swept through the area. Builder John Wardrop put up a new tenement here and gave the resulting court and its archway his own name.
interesting_fact: The court sits immediately beside Lady Stair's Close and Makars' Court, part of the same cluster of Old Town redevelopment carried out as the Lawnmarket was remodelled in the late 19th century.

title: Author's Phrases in the Flagstones
address: Lady Stair's Cl & Makars' Ct, Edinburgh EH1 2LP, UK
about_site_text: The flagstones of Makars' Court, in the courtyard beside the Writers' Museum, are inscribed with quotations from more than one hundred Scottish writers, from medieval makars to contemporary poets. Each inscription is chosen by a committee and unveiled at an annual ceremony, slowly building the court into a permanent literary map carved directly into the ground.
interesting_fact: New quotations are still being added today - Makars' Court is a living monument, not a fixed one, with fresh inscriptions unveiled most years to honour Scottish writers old and new.

title: Scottish War Poets Memorial
address: Lady Stair's Cl & Makars' Ct, Edinburgh EH1 2LP, UK
about_site_text: This hand-carved Celtic cross in light grey granite, its shaft decorated with deep Celtic knotwork and a stone sword in relief, was unveiled in Makars' Court in November 2018 to commemorate Scotland's First World War poets. It was installed jointly by Edinburgh Napier University, the University of Aberdeen, the Scottish Poetry Library, and the National Library of Scotland, among other partners.
interesting_fact: The memorial's inscription is a line of verse: 'Sweet be their sleep now wherever they're lying, far though they be from the hills of their home' - a tribute to Scottish soldier-poets who died far from home in the trenches.

title: Milne's Court
about_site_text: Milne's Court, built in 1692 by Robert Milne, master mason to the king, was the first open courtyard of its kind in Edinburgh - a deliberate break from the cramped, enclosed closes surrounding it. The original west range was demolished in 1883, but the University of Edinburgh restored the north and south blocks and rebuilt the east range between 1966 and 1970, turning the court into student accommodation.
interesting_fact: Milne's Court set the template that later, grander courtyards like James' Court and Riddle's Court would follow - proof that even in the crowded 17th-century Old Town, there was appetite for a bit more light and air.

title: James' Court
about_site_text: James' Court was built from 1727 by James Brownhill, from whom it takes its name, and quickly became one of Edinburgh's most fashionable addresses - philosopher David Hume lived here before moving to the New Town, and diarist James Boswell later took over Hume's old flat. The buildings behind Gladstone's Land, some dating to the 16th century, still convey the crowded feel of the 18th-century Old Town.
interesting_fact: James Boswell entertained Samuel Johnson here during Johnson's 1773 visit to Edinburgh, the very trip that produced Johnson's 'A Journey to the Western Islands of Scotland'.

title: The Jolly Judge
about_site_text: Tucked below street level just off the Lawnmarket, the Jolly Judge is a traditional basement pub known for its low beamed ceilings and roaring log fire - a world away from the busier tourist bars further down the Royal Mile. Its location close to the Sheriff Court and High Court once made it a favourite haunt of the city's legal community.
interesting_fact: In 2024 the Jolly Judge was named CAMRA Edinburgh Pub of the Year and also picked up Cider Pub of the Year, recognition for a pub that deliberately keeps the music off to stay a genuinely quiet place to drink.

title: Susannah Alice Stephen Memorial
about_site_text: This memorial seat, topped with a bronze sculpture of a parakeet and garden trug by sculptor Frances Pelly, sits in James' Court in honour of Susannah Alice Stephen (1960-1997), a landscape designer who co-founded the Scottish Society of Garden Designers before her death in a diving accident off the Galapagos Islands. She chose this spot deliberately, knowing that pioneering town planner Patrick Geddes - a hero of hers for bringing green space into Edinburgh's Old Town - had once lived in James' Court himself.
interesting_fact: The memorial is inscribed with the line 'Keep your face towards the sun and the shadows will fall behind you', a fitting motto for a landscape designer who spent her career finding light and green space within the dense, shadowed closes of the Old Town.

title: The Ensign Ewart
about_site_text: This Lawnmarket pub, trading in some form since at least 1680, was renamed in 1938 in honour of Ensign Charles Ewart of the Royal Scots Greys, who captured the eagle standard of the French 45th Regiment of the Line at the Battle of Waterloo in 1815. The name was chosen the same year Ewart's remains were reburied with full honours at Edinburgh Castle.
interesting_fact: A large painting of the Battle of Waterloo hangs inside, alongside Scottish military memorabilia - the pub sits only a few hundred metres from Ewart's actual grave on the Castle esplanade.

title: Boswell's Court
about_site_text: Boswell's Court on Castlehill dates from the 17th century and takes its name not from the famous diarist James Boswell but from his uncle, Dr John Boswell, a physician who lived here. James did visit his uncle at this address in October 1762, and a plaque on the building - now home to the Witchery restaurant - also claims that James Boswell and Samuel Johnson dined here around 1770.
interesting_fact: The stair entrance still carries a carved lintel bearing a merchant's mark and the initials 'T' and 'L', thought to belong to an earlier owner, Thomas Lowthian.

title: Ramsay Lane
about_site_text: Ramsay Lane climbs steeply from the Royal Mile up toward the Castle esplanade, named for the poet Allan Ramsay, whose distinctive octagonal house - nicknamed 'the goose-pie house' for its unusual shape - once stood at its head. The lane connects Castlehill to Ramsay Garden, the striking Arts and Crafts tenement development built around Ramsay's old home in the 1890s.
interesting_fact: Ramsay Garden was one of the first projects of town planner Patrick Geddes, who saw restoring housing on the Castle slopes as a way to bring the professional classes back to live in the Old Town.

title: Castle Rock Hostel
about_site_text: This 19th-century Johnston Terrace building was originally constructed as a school and teacher training college before becoming Castle Rock Hostel in 1997. Its interiors lean fully into a medieval theme, with pointed arches, faux tapestries, heraldic shields, and suits of armour lining the stairs, all within sight of the Castle esplanade just above.
interesting_fact: The hostel now hosts around 40,000 overnight guests a year and underwent a major renovation that added a dramatic new staircase to open up extra accommodation in the attic, while keeping the historic exterior intact.

title: St Columba's by the Castle
about_site_text: St Columba's by the Castle was built in 1846-47 in Early English Gothic style to designs by architect John Henderson, using stone brought from the demolished palace of Mary of Guise on the Royal Mile. Its layout reflects the reforming ideas of the Oxford Movement within the Scottish Episcopal Church, and a day school beneath the church once educated up to 200 local children.
interesting_fact: The church's east window, blocked up for decades, was eventually filled in 1959 with a striking mural of 'Christ Enthroned' by artist John Busby.

title: Fiddler's Arms
about_site_text: The Fiddler's Arms sits at the western end of the Grassmarket, in the shadow of Edinburgh Castle, on a stretch of the Old Town once dominated by the wholesale trade running through the neighbouring West Bow - merchants here dealt in iron, pitch, tar, hemp, and other heavy goods bound for warehouses down in Leith.
interesting_fact: True to its name, the pub still leans into a folk-music identity, with regular traditional Scottish sessions - a nod to a Grassmarket long associated with market traders, drovers, and travelling entertainers.

title: West Port Garden
about_site_text: West Port Garden was created in 1909 by pioneering town planner Patrick Geddes as one of several small green spaces he carved into the crowded Old Town, specifically to give slum children a place to experience nature. His daughter Norah, a landscape gardener, designed the terraced plot on the steep slope between West Port and the College of Art, and it officially opened in June 1910.
interesting_fact: Over a century later the garden is still community-run, now overseen by the Grassmarket Residents Association, and continues to host local people doing therapeutic gardening and growing their own food.

title: Portsburgh Square
about_site_text: Portsburgh Square is a pocket of mid-20th-century social housing tucked behind the Grassmarket, its balconied, pastel-painted tenement blocks built directly beneath the sheer face of Castle Rock. The square takes its name from the old Burgh of Portsburgh, an independent burgh that grew up outside Edinburgh's city walls near the West Port before being absorbed into the city in the 19th century.
interesting_fact: Standing in the square gives one of the most dramatic close-up views of Edinburgh Castle anywhere in the city, with the volcanic crag rising almost directly overhead.

title: Salvation Army Womens Hostel
about_site_text: This Art Nouveau-detailed building on West Port was built in 1910-11 to designs by Glasgow architect John Hamilton as a Salvation Army hostel for homeless and vulnerable women, with its foundation stone laid by a senior Salvation Army officer on 6 February 1911. Carved lettering reading 'THE SALVATION ARMY WOMENS HOSTEL' still runs across the facade above the entrance.
interesting_fact: The building has since been converted into backpacker accommodation, now trading as Kick Ass Hostels, though its original carved signage remains as a visible reminder of over a century of sheltering the city's most vulnerable residents.

title: Granny's Green Steps
about_site_text: Granny's Green Steps climb from the Grassmarket up to Johnston Terrace, cutting through what was once a communal drying green - 'Granny's Green' - used by the wives of soldiers from the Castle's married quarters to hang out their washing in the 19th century. Despite the old-fashioned name, the steps themselves are a modern addition, rebuilt in 2001.
interesting_fact: Nobody now knows for certain who 'Granny' was - some think the sign should actually read 'Granny Green's Steps', after a specific named resident, rather than a generic grandmother.

title: Quaker Meeting House
address: 7 Victoria Terrace, above, Victoria St, Edinburgh EH1 2JL, UK
about_site_text: This Italian Gothic building on Victoria Terrace was built in 1865-66 as a chapel for the United Original Secession Church, then later served as headquarters for the Edinburgh Battalion of the Boys' Brigade. The Religious Society of Friends converted it into Edinburgh's Quaker Meeting House in 1987, giving the city's Quaker community - which had first formed a small central Edinburgh meeting back in 1924 - a permanent, fully accessible home.
interesting_fact: Before settling here, Edinburgh's Central Meeting spent almost fifty years, from 1938 to 1987, gathering in a building on Stafford Street in the New Town.

title: The Albanach
about_site_text: The Albanach takes its Gaelic name - meaning 'Scottish' or 'Highlander' - seriously, stocking over 330 different malt whiskies behind its High Street bar. Behind the pub's stone-walled front room, a quieter restaurant serves modern Scottish food, giving the building a split identity: buzzing whisky bar facing the Royal Mile, calmer dining room tucked away from it.
interesting_fact: With well over 300 malts on the shelf, the Albanach's whisky list is one of the largest on the entire Royal Mile - a serious collection for a street already packed with whisky bars.

title: The Advocate
about_site_text: The Advocate sits on Hunter Square right beside St Giles' Cathedral, converted into a pub in the 1990s in a building that takes its name from the legal profession clustered nearby around Parliament House. It reopened after a refit in May 2025, and still draws a daytime crowd of lawyers on their lunch break alongside the usual Old Town foot traffic.
interesting_fact: The pub can seat over 200 people and runs live music through the week - acoustic sets on Sunday nights, livelier entertainment on Fridays - a scale that's easy to miss from its fairly modest Hunter Square frontage.

title: Malt Shovel Inn
about_site_text: The Malt Shovel occupies a building dating to around 1800 on Cockburn Street, a curving Victorian street cut through the Old Town in the 1850s specifically to give better carriage access up to the newly built Waverley Station. Inside, the pub keeps its period character - corniced ceilings, dark woodwork, and stained glass - across three connected rooms.
interesting_fact: Cockburn Street itself is a rare piece of deliberate town planning slotted into the organic, centuries-old street pattern of the Old Town - built purely to solve a 19th-century traffic problem.

title: The Piper's Rest
about_site_text: The Piper's Rest sits on Hunter Square just behind the Tron Kirk, serving Scottish food - haggis, Cullen skink, steak pie - alongside a solid range of malt whiskies, local gins, and craft beers. Live music runs seven nights a week, mixing traditional Scottish tunes with more contemporary covers.
interesting_fact: The pub's golden bagpiper figures displayed in its window cases give it one of the more eye-catching frontages on Hunter Square, visible from the top of the square day or night.

title: The Scotsman's Lounge
about_site_text: The Scotsman's Lounge has been trading as a pub on Cockburn Street since 1860, making it one of the older continuously running pubs on this stretch of the Old Town. Its traditional interior keeps a small stage area for live musicians, who perform most evenings, and it sells a large range of malt whiskies just a couple of minutes' walk from the Royal Mile.
interesting_fact: The pub's reopening after a refurbishment was significant enough locally that the City of Edinburgh Council's own leader issued a public welcome for it - a nod to how much these small independent Cockburn Street venues matter to the area's identity.
